dogs-camping-new-zealand.title: Camping with a dog in New Zealand
dogs-camping-new-zealand.description: Conservation land, council reserves and holiday parks have different permissions even when the dog stays in a vehicle.
dogs-camping-new-zealand.imageAlt: Dog on lead beside a legal New Zealand campsite
dogs-camping-new-zealand.intro: Dog access must be checked for the exact land. Native wildlife protection means many conservation areas prohibit pets completely, including animals left inside a vehicle.

sections.heading: DOC rules are strict
body: Pets are generally not allowed at DOC camps, huts, lodges or cottages without written approval. Some campsites expressly allow dogs under listed conditions, but national parks remain no-dog environments.
A dog may travel to a hut only where dog access is allowed and must remain outside the hut. Search the exact place page before departure.

sections.heading: Councils and private parks
body: Council camping areas can combine freedom-camping bylaws with separate dog-control rules. A site may allow a vehicle overnight but prohibit dogs in the reserve.
Holiday parks set their own conditions, often by season, size or site type. Confirm in writing and disclose every animal when booking.

sections.heading: Protect wildlife and neighbours
body: Use a lead where required, prevent barking and collect all waste. Keep dogs away from nesting birds, seals, livestock and pest-control poison zones.
Carry vaccination information and a secure restraint for travel. If access is unclear, choose a dog-friendly commercial site rather than testing the rule on arrival.

sections.heading: Most conservation land is closed to dogs
body: Dogs are prohibited on the large majority of public conservation land, including most national parks, because kiwi and other ground-nesting birds have no defence against them. A single dog off a lead has killed multiple kiwi in a night, and this is why the restriction is absolute rather than discretionary.

A limited number of DOC areas permit dogs, and some require a permit obtained in advance. Check the specific place before you travel rather than assuming, because the penalties are significant and the risk to wildlife is real.
tips: Most national parks ban dogs entirely
Some areas need a permit in advance
Check the specific site, never assume

sections.heading: 1080 and pest control operations
body: Aerial 1080 is used widely for possum and rat control and is lethal to dogs, both directly and through eating poisoned carcasses, with the risk persisting for months after an operation. Warning signs are posted at access points and operations are published in advance.

Check for current and recent operations along your route before travelling with a dog, and keep it leashed and muzzled where advised. This is the single largest avoidable risk to a dog on a New Zealand trip.

sections.heading: Holiday parks and council reserves
body: Many holiday parks accept dogs but a substantial number do not, and those that do frequently exclude them during peak season or require them to be crated or leashed at all times. Booking without confirming the policy is a common way to arrive with nowhere to stay.

Council reserves and beaches often have seasonal dog restrictions protecting nesting shorebirds, typically over spring and summer. These are signed locally and enforced, and they change between neighbouring councils.
tips: Confirm the dog policy when booking
Peak season exclusions are common
Beach restrictions protect nesting birds

sections.heading: Practical travel with a dog
body: A dog must be restrained in a vehicle, and travelling on the back of a ute requires proper securing. Heat in a parked vehicle kills quickly here, and shade moves, so a dog cannot be left while you do a walk that excludes them.

Plan the trip around the places that accept dogs rather than hoping to improvise. In practice that usually means coastal walkways, forestry tracks, regional parks and holiday parks rather than national parks and Great Walks.

sections.heading: Where a dog can actually go
body: In practice the workable options are holiday parks that accept dogs, council reserves outside restricted seasons, forestry and regional park tracks, and most beaches outside nesting periods. That is a real trip, but it is a different trip from one built around national parks.

Several regional parks around Auckland and Wellington allow dogs on lead, and many coastal walkways permit them year-round. These tend to be places where kiwi and ground-nesting birds are absent or already fenced out.

Plan the route around the dog-friendly places first and fill in around them. Attempting a standard South Island itinerary with a dog produces a trip where somebody waits in the vehicle for most of the good walks.

sections.heading: Kiwi aversion training
body: Some regions offer kiwi aversion training for dogs, and in a few areas it is a condition of access. It is worth doing for any dog spending time in Northland, Coromandel or the West Coast even where it is not required.
Even a trained dog must be under control. Most kiwi killed by dogs are killed by pets whose owners were certain their animal would not chase anything.
tips: Aversion training is required in some areas
Trained dogs still need control
Most incidents involve pets, not strays

faq: Can you take a dog camping in New Zealand?

In some places. Dogs are banned from almost all national parks and most conservation land because of the risk to native birds, and kiwi live in places that look nothing like a sanctuary. Holiday parks and a subset of council reserves do allow them.
Where are dogs banned in New Zealand?
As a working rule: national parks, most DOC land, all kiwi habitat and most regional bird reserves. Where a dog is allowed on conservation land it is usually under a permit and always on a lead.

kauri-dieback-camping-travel.title: Kauri dieback: clean gear before northern camps and walks
kauri-dieback-camping-travel.description: Soil on boots, tent pegs and tyres can carry a pathogen that kills kauri trees.
kauri-dieback-camping-travel.intro: Kauri dieback moves in contaminated soil and has no cure. Camping gear creates many contact points, so cleaning only hiking boots is not enough.

sections.heading: Arrive clean
body: Scrub every visible clump of soil from footwear, poles, tent pegs, mats, bike tyres and tools before entering kauri country. Clean at home or another suitable hard surface where wash water cannot reach the forest.
Use every hygiene station in the direction shown, even when equipment looks clean. Disinfectant works only after soil has been removed.

sections.heading: Stay on open tracks
body: Obey closures, barriers and boardwalk instructions. Stepping around mud widens the contaminated area and can move soil toward kauri roots.
Choose another walk when a track is closed. An old guide or GPS line does not authorise access through a protection zone.

sections.heading: Clean between regions
body: Repeat cleaning before leaving a forest area and before the next kauri catchment. Store dirty equipment separately until it can be treated properly.
Dogs can also move contaminated soil and may be prohibited for additional conservation reasons. Check both kauri and pet rules.

sections.heading: How the disease actually spreads
body: Kauri dieback is caused by a soil-borne pathogen that moves in a single gram of soil on a boot, a tent peg, a bike tyre or a dog's paws. There is no cure and infected trees die. The spread is almost entirely human-assisted, which is why the hygiene stations exist.

The critical part is mechanical: you must physically scrub the soil off before the disinfectant does anything. Spraying over caked mud achieves nothing at all, and this is the step most visitors skip.
tips: Scrub the soil off first, then spray
One gram of soil can carry it
Spraying over mud does nothing

sections.heading: Stay on the structures
body: In kauri forest the boardwalks and matting are not a convenience, they are the containment. Stepping off to pass someone, to take a photograph or to reach a better angle puts soil onto your boots from within the root zone, which extends well beyond the visible canopy.
Kauri roots are shallow and wide, and compaction damages them directly as well as spreading the pathogen. The structures exist because walking on the ground near a kauri harms it twice.

sections.heading: Some tracks are closed permanently
body: Large parts of the Waitākere Ranges and other northern forests have been closed under rāhui and formal closures, and some will not reopen. Old blog posts and guidebooks describing these walks circulate widely and are no longer accurate.
Check the current DOC and Auckland Council status before planning a walk to a specific tree or track. Entering a closed area is both an offence and a direct threat to the stand it is protecting.
tips: Old guides list closed tracks
Check DOC and council status first
Rāhui closures are not advisory

sections.heading: Clean gear before you arrive, not just between tracks
body: Arriving in Northland or the Coromandel with soil from another region on your boots is how the pathogen moves between forests. Clean and dry footwear, tent pegs, poles and groundsheets before you travel north, not only at the track entrance.

The same applies to vehicles on unsealed forestry roads and to dogs, which are prohibited in most kauri areas partly for this reason. Treat soil as the thing you are managing rather than mud as an inconvenience.

sections.heading: Why it matters beyond the trees
body: Kauri are foundation species: entire communities of plants, fungi and invertebrates depend on them and some exist nowhere else. Losing a stand is not losing trees, it is losing the system built around them over centuries.

They are also taonga, with individual trees named and carrying whakapapa and history. Tane Mahuta and Te Matua Ngahere are not tourist attractions in the ordinary sense, and the rahui placed over affected forests reflect that standing.

The hygiene measures ask very little of any individual visitor. Thirty seconds at a cleaning station and staying on a boardwalk is the entire contribution required, and it is currently the only thing slowing the spread.

sections.heading: What to do if you find a sick tree
body: Symptoms include yellowing foliage, canopy thinning, dead branches and a gum bleed at the base of the trunk. If you see them, note the location and report it rather than approaching for a closer look.
Do not take samples, touch the bleeding gum or move soil away from the tree. Reporting through DOC or the regional council is genuinely useful, because surveillance depends heavily on public reports.
tips: Gum bleed at the trunk base is the sign
Report it, do not investigate
Never move soil near a sick tree

faq: What is kauri dieback and why does it matter to campers?
It is a soil-borne disease that kills kauri and has no cure. It moves in a pinch of dirt on a boot or a tyre, which makes visitors the main way it spreads between forests.
How do you clean gear for kauri dieback?

Scrub all soil off boots, poles, tyres and dog paws before and after every visit, then use the disinfectant stations at track entrances. Removing the soil is the part that works, and disinfectant on a muddy boot does nothing.

new-zealand-biosecurity-camping-gear.title: NZ Biosecurity: Declare Hiking Boots and Camping Gear
new-zealand-biosecurity-camping-gear.description: Used boots, tents and fishing gear must be declared when you arrive in New Zealand. What to clean before you fly and how to stop pests between rivers.
new-zealand-biosecurity-camping-gear.imageAlt: Clean hiking boots prepared for New Zealand biosecurity
new-zealand-biosecurity-camping-gear.intro: Used outdoor equipment can carry seeds, soil, insects and aquatic pests. Biosecurity starts at the border and continues when gear moves between New Zealand ecosystems.

sections.heading: Declare on arrival
body: Declare used boots, tents, fishing equipment, food, plant material and animal products when required by the New Zealand Traveller Declaration. A declaration lets officers assess and clean items; concealment creates the risk and penalty.
Pack gear where it can be inspected easily. Scrub soil and plant material before flying, but still declare the item when the question applies.

sections.heading: Clean between places
body: Check, clean and dry boats, waders, paddles and fishing gear before another waterway. Microscopic pests survive in moisture that appears harmless.
Brush seeds and mud from tyres, pegs and walking gear before changing catchments. Use local wash stations where supplied.

sections.heading: Do not improvise disposal
body: Never release bait, aquarium water, food plants or untreated wash water into the environment. Use rubbish and wastewater systems designed for the material.
Follow regional pest-control notices and temporary rāhui. Local restrictions may protect a species or place beyond the national minimum.

sections.heading: Declare everything at the border
body: New Zealand's biosecurity regime is among the strictest anywhere and instant fines apply for undeclared risk goods. Used hiking boots, tents, camping equipment, bicycles and anything that has been in soil or fresh water must be declared, and food of almost any kind must be declared.

Declaring costs nothing and takes a minute. The officer may inspect and clean the item and send you on your way. Failing to declare is what produces the fine, not the item itself, and the distinction catches out a lot of well-meaning visitors.
tips: Declaring is free, not declaring is fined
Used boots and tents must be declared
All food must be declared

sections.heading: Clean gear before you pack it
body: Arrive with boots scrubbed free of soil, tents dry and free of seeds and insects, and any water-contact equipment cleaned and dried. Gear that arrives visibly dirty is more likely to be held for treatment, which can mean collecting it later or losing it.
Check pockets and stuff sacks for seeds, leaf litter and dried mud. A tent packed damp in another country frequently arrives with a colony of something, and it is easier to deal with at home.

sections.heading: Check, Clean, Dry between waterways
body: Didymo and other freshwater pests move on damp gear between catchments. The requirement applies to boots, waders, tents, fishing equipment, paddleboards and anything else that has been in fresh water, and it applies within New Zealand as much as at the border.
Clean thoroughly, then dry completely and leave it dry for at least 48 hours before entering another waterway. Where drying is not practical, use the recommended treatment solutions instead.
tips: Applies within New Zealand, not just entry
Dry for 48 hours before the next waterway
Covers boots, tents and boards

sections.heading: Moving between islands and regions
body: There are internal controls too. Ulva Island, Rakiura and other predator-free sanctuaries require you to check bags for rodents and seeds before boarding, and the checking stations at the wharves are not a formality. A single rat reaching an island undoes decades of work.

Fruit fly and other regional controls occasionally restrict moving fresh produce within the country. Where a control area is in force it is signed and publicised, and the rules apply to a campervan fridge as much as to a truck.

sections.heading: Why the rules are this strict
body: New Zealand's native species evolved with no land mammals and almost no defences against them. Introduced predators, weeds and diseases have already caused extinctions, and the border controls exist because the country is still losing species to things that arrive in luggage.

Foot and mouth, fruit fly and myrtle rust are the incursions with the largest economic and ecological consequences, and each has been intercepted at the border more than once. The inspection you find inconvenient is the reason those interceptions happen.
The process is quick and officers are helpful when you declare. The penalty is for concealment rather than for owning muddy boots, and the difference is entirely in whether you tick the box.

sections.heading: Leaving the country again
body: Some items you acquire here cannot leave, and others need paperwork. Anything made from protected species, greenstone taken from certain areas, and some plant material all carry restrictions worth checking before you pack.
Australia in particular has its own strict border rules, so gear that arrives here muddy will face the same scrutiny on the way out. Clean everything again before the return flight.
tips: Check restrictions before taking items out
Australia is equally strict inbound
Clean gear again before flying home

faq: What camping gear has to be declared at the New Zealand border?

Tents, boots, hiking poles, bikes and anything else that has touched soil or fresh water overseas, along with food, seeds and wooden items. Declaring costs nothing; failing to declare carries an instant fine.
How should you prepare gear before flying to New Zealand?

Clean it before you pack. Soil removed from boots and tent pegs at home, and a bike or a pack dried and brushed, is the difference between a two-minute inspection and having your gear treated or confiscated.

sandflies-new-zealand-camping.title: Sandfly Bites in NZ: How to Camp With Fewer of Them
sandflies-new-zealand-camping.description: Repellent, clothing, pitch choice and a closed-door arrival routine for the West Coast, Fiordland and damp bush camps where sandflies bite most.
sandflies-new-zealand-camping.intro: Sandflies are most intense around damp, sheltered water edges, especially on the West Coast and in Fiordland. They are irritating rather than a reason to avoid the region, but small camp habits make a large difference.

sections.heading: Choose the pitch carefully
body: Moving air and distance from still water can reduce activity. Keep doors and screens closed before unloading, because an open campervan becomes a trap for the rest of the night.
Wear long sleeves, socks and trousers at dawn and dusk. Apply an effective repellent according to its label and reapply after swimming or heavy rain.

sections.heading: Manage the interior
body: Repair screen holes before reaching remote camps and avoid bright interior lights with doors open. Cook outside only as conditions allow, then move inside quickly.
Do not spray insecticide around food, children or unventilated sleeping spaces. Use products only where their directions permit.

sections.heading: Treat bites and watch reactions
body: Wash bites, avoid scratching and use ordinary itch relief when suitable. Seek medical advice for signs of infection or a severe allergic reaction.
Sandfly pressure changes with wind, temperature and rainfall. A nearby exposed holiday park can be a sensible alternative to a beautiful but still riverside camp.

sections.heading: Where and when they are worst
body: Sandflies concentrate on the West Coast, throughout Fiordland, around the Catlins and in damp bush near water anywhere in the country. They are worst at dawn and dusk, in still conditions and close to rivers and coast, and they largely disappear in wind, cold and full sun.

The transition can be abrupt. The eastern side of the Haast Pass is close to sandfly-free and the western descent is not, so have repellent accessible in the cab rather than packed away before you cross.
tips: West Coast, Fiordland, Catlins are worst
Dawn, dusk and still air
Wind and cold suppress them

sections.heading: What actually works
body: Repellents containing DEET or picaridin are the effective options, applied to skin before you leave the vehicle rather than after the first bites. Reapply after swimming or sweating, and cover ankles, wrists and the back of the neck, which is where most bites land.
Physical barriers work better than chemistry. Long sleeves, long trousers and socks in the evening remove most of the problem, and a head net is not an overreaction on the Milford road in summer.

sections.heading: Managing the tent and the vehicle
body: Check the insect mesh for holes before you travel, because a single tear makes the tent useless against them. Enter and exit quickly, and get in the habit of zipping fully rather than most of the way.

Sandflies follow you into a van and stay. Closing up before dusk rather than after it, and killing the few that got in before you settle, saves a long night. A small battery fan disrupts their flight and helps more than it sounds.
tips: Check the mesh before you leave home
Close up before dusk, not after
A small fan genuinely helps

sections.heading: Treating the bites
body: The reaction is delayed and the itch peaks a day or two later, often lasting a week. Antihistamine cream or tablets help, as does not scratching, which is easier said than done and is what turns a bite into an infected sore.

Some people react far more strongly than others, and reactions can build over a trip rather than settle. Carry treatment with you rather than planning to buy it, because the places where you need it are the places with no pharmacy.

sections.heading: Planning a trip around them
body: On the West Coast and in Fiordland, choose sites with some exposure to breeze rather than tucked into sheltered bush beside a river. The most beautiful sheltered spot is reliably the worst one, and a slightly windier pitch makes for a far better evening.

Time your outdoor tasks. Setting up camp, cooking and eating are all much easier in the middle of the day or in wind than at dusk, so arriving early is worth more here than almost anywhere else in the country.

Maori tradition holds that Hine-nui-te-po released the namu at Milford to stop people lingering and becoming too enchanted by the place. Having spent an evening there without repellent, the story is hard to argue with.

sections.heading: What does not work
body: Citronella candles, ultrasonic devices and wristbands are all widely sold and none of them meaningfully reduce bites. Neither does eating garlic or taking vitamin B, despite how often both are recommended.
Spend the money on a proper repellent and long sleeves instead. The things that work are unglamorous and reliable, and the things that do not are the ones sold at the campground shop.
tips: Citronella and wristbands do not work
Ultrasonic devices are useless
DEET or picaridin plus clothing

faq: Where are sandflies worst in New Zealand?
The West Coast, Fiordland and the wetter parts of the south, particularly near water at dawn and dusk. They are almost absent in dry inland country and on windy open coast.
What actually works against sandflies?

Covered skin and a repellent containing DEET or picaridin, reapplied. They cannot fly well in wind or in an enclosed tent, so choosing an exposed site and keeping the mesh shut does more than any spray.

new-zealand-severe-weather-camping.title: Severe weather and camping in New Zealand
new-zealand-severe-weather-camping.description: Official warnings, river levels and shelter matter more than the icon in an ordinary forecast.
new-zealand-severe-weather-camping.imageAlt: Dark storm clouds over a New Zealand campsite
new-zealand-severe-weather-camping.intro: New Zealand weather can shift from local inconvenience to road closure or evacuation. Campers need to connect the warning to the exact valley, coast, river and road rather than treating rain as a uniform national event.

sections.heading: Use official warnings
body: Check MetService severe weather information and local Civil Defence channels before departure and during any active system. Waka Kotahi and councils provide the road consequences.
Weather at a nearby town may not describe an alpine pass or coastal camp. Read the warning area and expected timing.

sections.heading: Move before conditions peak
body: Leave river flats, low coastal ground and exposed forest camps early when authorities advise it. Do not wait for visible flooding or falling branches to confirm the forecast.
Park facing a safe exit without blocking others. Keep keys, shoes, warm layers and essential medication ready.

sections.heading: After the storm
body: Assume fords, slips and unsealed roads may remain unsafe after rain ends. Never drive through floodwater or around a closure.
Recheck drinking-water notices and campground status. A calm morning does not prove damaged access has reopened.

sections.heading: Weather here changes faster than the forecast
body: New Zealand sits in the path of systems crossing the Tasman with nothing to slow them, and conditions can shift completely within an hour. A forecast for a town tells you relatively little about a pass, an exposed coast or a valley twenty minutes away.

Check MetService for the specific location rather than the region, and check again in the morning before committing to an exposed site or an alpine road. Treat a forecast more than two days out as an indication rather than a plan.
tips: Check the location, not the region
Recheck each morning
Two-day forecasts are indications

sections.heading: Wind is the most common problem
body: More camping trips are damaged by wind than by rain. Awnings left out, tents pitched broadside and roof vents left open account for most of it, and wind commonly rises through the evening rather than dropping off at dusk.

Pitch with the smallest profile into the wind, use every guyline rather than the minimum, and bring awnings in before you go to bed rather than when they start moving. Choose shelter over the view when the forecast is strong.

sections.heading: Flooding and river flats
body: Braided riverbeds and low river flats look like ideal camping and are the most dangerous ground available in heavy rain. Rivers here rise extremely quickly, and rain falling in the headwaters hours away and out of sight is what catches people out.

Camp above the obvious flood level, never on a gravel bar or island, and leave if the water starts rising or discolouring. Do not attempt to drive through floodwater; the depth and whether the road is still under it are both unknowable from the vehicle.
tips: Never camp on a gravel bar
Rain upstream floods clear skies
Never drive through floodwater

sections.heading: Warnings and what to do with them
body: MetService issues watches and warnings, Civil Defence publishes emergency advice, NZTA covers road closures and DOC posts track and campsite alerts. Between them they cover everything that would change your plans, and they need checking while you still have signal.

When a severe weather warning covers your area, move to a serviced campground, a cabin or a town. That is not an overreaction: exposed camping in a genuine New Zealand storm is unpleasant at best and dangerous at worst.

sections.heading: Making the call to move
body: The decision people get wrong is staying put because moving feels like abandoning the plan. Relocating to a serviced campground, a cabin or a town before a front arrives costs a night's fee and a short drive, and it removes almost all of the risk.

Make the call while you still have daylight and reception rather than once conditions have started. Driving out of an exposed site in a rising storm after dark is considerably worse than either staying put or having left earlier.

Identify a specific fallback for each region instead of a vague intention to find something. Knowing the name of the holiday park and that it has space is what makes the decision easy at the moment you need to make it.

sections.heading: After the weather passes
body: Slips, fallen trees and washed-out fords can persist for days after the rain stops, and road openings lag behind the forecast. Check conditions again before moving rather than assuming a clear morning means a clear route.
Rivers stay high and discoloured well after the rain, so crossings that looked fine on the way in may not be on the way out. Rebuild the day around what the road and river are doing, not the sky.
tips: Roads reopen after the weather clears
Rivers stay high for longer
Recheck before moving on

faq: How much warning do New Zealand storms give?
Often less than a day. Weather here can turn from settled to severe in hours, particularly on the West Coast and in the exhausted alpine passes, so a forecast checked yesterday is not a plan.
What should you do if a severe weather warning is issued while camping?

Move off riverbanks, beaches and under trees, and get to a town or a sheltered formal campground rather than sitting it out. Road closures follow storms quickly, so leaving early is usually the only option you get.

earthquake-tsunami-camping-new-zealand.title: Earthquakes and tsunami safety for New Zealand campers
earthquake-tsunami-camping-new-zealand.description: Know the evacuation route before sleeping on the coast and act on natural warning signs immediately.
earthquake-tsunami-camping-new-zealand.imageAlt: Tsunami evacuation route sign on the New Zealand coast
earthquake-tsunami-camping-new-zealand.intro: Many memorable camps sit close to the sea. Before nightfall, identify whether the place lies in a tsunami evacuation zone and where higher ground can be reached without depending on a vehicle.

sections.heading: Before the shaking
body: Use local evacuation maps and signs to find the route and safe area. Keep shoes, torch, warm clothing and essential medication easy to grab.
Do not park across an evacuation path. In a crowded coast camp, walking can be faster and safer than joining a vehicle queue.

sections.heading: Stay away until cleared
body: Tsunami waves can continue for hours and the first may not be the largest. Remain outside the zone until officials give the all-clear.
Expect damaged roads and power loss. Use radio and official channels, conserve phone battery and help others without returning to collect equipment.

sections.heading: Long or strong, get gone
body: This is the official rule and it is worth memorising exactly. If an earthquake at the coast lasts longer than a minute, or is strong enough that you cannot stand up, move immediately to high ground or as far inland as you can. Do not wait for an official warning, because for a local-source tsunami there will not be time for one.

Go on foot if the ground allows it, because roads jam and bridges may be damaged. Aim for at least 35 metres above sea level or a kilometre inland, and stay there until officials say it is safe rather than returning after the first wave.
tips: Long or strong, get gone
Do not wait for an official warning
35 m up or 1 km inland, on foot

sections.heading: Choosing a coastal campsite with this in mind
body: When you arrive at a coastal site, spend a minute identifying the way to high ground. Many New Zealand coastal areas have marked tsunami evacuation routes and blue lines showing the safe zone boundary, and knowing where yours is costs nothing.

This matters most on the East Coast, Kaikōura, Wellington's south coast and the Bay of Plenty, all of which face significant local-source risk. It applies to a beachfront holiday park as much as a remote DOC site.

sections.heading: During the shaking
body: Drop, cover and hold on. In a tent, stay put and protect your head; the tent itself is unlikely to hurt you. In a campervan, stay inside and hold on rather than trying to get out, and if you are driving, pull over clear of bridges, banks and power lines and stay in the vehicle.

Expect aftershocks, sometimes for weeks. After a significant shake, check for damage to your site, avoid slopes and cliff bases that may now be unstable, and be cautious around any structure that has moved.
tips: Drop, cover, hold on
Stay in the vehicle if driving
Aftershocks continue for weeks

sections.heading: Being prepared to be self-sufficient
body: A significant earthquake can close roads, cut power and disrupt fuel and water supply for days, and in a remote area you may be genuinely on your own for a while. Carrying water, food, warm clothing, a torch and a charged power bank covers most of it.

Keep the fuel tank above half in seismically active regions where practical, and know that mobile networks may be congested or down. A battery radio is a genuinely useful item, because emergency broadcasting continues when the network does not.

sections.heading: Why this is worth thinking about here
body: New Zealand straddles an active tectonic plate boundary, records thousands of earthquakes a year and has a documented history of large local-source tsunami. The 2016 Kaikoura earthquake generated waves within minutes of the shaking.

For a local-source event no warning system can help in time. The shaking itself is the warning, which is why the official advice is built entirely around what you do without being told anything by anyone.
None of this should stop anyone camping on the coast. It takes one minute on arrival to work out where high ground is, and that single habit covers the whole risk.

sections.heading: Distant-source tsunami
body: A tsunami generated far away gives hours of warning, and official alerts will reach you through Civil Defence, radio and emergency mobile alerts. That is the situation where waiting for instruction is correct.

The distinction matters: local-source means move immediately without waiting, distant-source means follow the official advice. Knowing which one you are in comes down to whether you felt the earthquake yourself.
tips: Felt it? Move immediately
Did not feel it? Follow official advice
Emergency mobile alerts reach most phones

faq: What should you do in an earthquake while camping in New Zealand?
Drop, cover and hold on, then check where you are. If you are on the coast and the shaking was long or strong enough that standing was hard, do not wait for an official warning.
When should you evacuate a coastal campsite for a tsunami?

Long or strong, get gone: if an earthquake lasts more than a minute or makes it hard to stand, move inland or to high ground immediately and on foot if the roads are jammed. Official warnings can arrive after the wave for a local source.

volcanic-safety-new-zealand-travel.title: Volcanic Safety NZ: GeoNet Alert Levels and Track Closures
volcanic-safety-new-zealand-travel.description: What GeoNet volcanic alerts mean for Tongariro, Ruapehu and Rotorua trips, how DOC closes tracks and how to stay safe around geothermal areas.
volcanic-safety-new-zealand-travel.imageAlt: Volcanic landscape in Tongariro National Park
volcanic-safety-new-zealand-travel.intro: Volcanic areas are active systems, not scenic sets. GeoNet alert levels, DOC closures and local operator instructions provide different parts of the safety picture and should all be checked.

sections.heading: Read current status
body: Review GeoNet volcanic alert information and DOC track notices before travelling. An alert level communicates activity, but it does not replace access restrictions for a specific walk.
Weather and volcanic hazards are separate. A low volcanic alert does not make an alpine crossing safe in high wind, snow or poor visibility.

sections.heading: Stay behind barriers
body: Geothermal crust can be thin and water can be near boiling. Remain on boardwalks and never step around a barrier for steam, colour or a photograph.
Keep children close and avoid touching pools, vents or runoff. Sulphur smell alone does not indicate the level of danger.

sections.heading: Have a changeable plan
body: Use shuttle and track operators that follow current access guidance. Carry layers, navigation and emergency supplies even on popular routes.
If activity closes a place, choose another region or lower walk. A holiday schedule never justifies crossing a closure.

sections.heading: The alert level system
body: GeoNet publishes a Volcanic Alert Level from 0 to 5 for each active volcano, and access restrictions follow it. Level 1 means minor unrest and is common at Ruapehu and White Island; level 2 and above bring closures of tracks and, at Tongariro, sections of the Alpine Crossing.

Check the current level for the specific volcano before you travel, not the region. Levels change with little notice, and a track that was open when you planned the trip may be closed by the time you arrive.
tips: Check GeoNet for the specific volcano
Level 2 and up closes tracks
Levels change with little notice

sections.heading: The Tongariro Alpine Crossing passes active vents
body: The Crossing runs close to Te Maari and the Red Crater area, and the route includes signed sections where you should not linger. Eruptions here have happened with no useful warning, including in 2012 when the track was damaged.

Follow the signage, do not stop for long in the marked hazard zones, and be prepared to turn back. The Crossing is also frequently closed or unsafe for weather reasons entirely separate from volcanic risk.

sections.heading: Geothermal ground is thinner than it looks
body: Around Rotorua, Taupō and Waiotapu the crust over boiling mud and water can be thin, and people have been very seriously injured stepping off marked paths. Ground that looks solid and dry can give way, and the water beneath is well above boiling.

Stay on the boardwalks and behind the barriers without exception, keep children in hand, and do not enter unmarked thermal areas even where there is no fence. Hydrogen sulphide also collects in hollows and can reach harmful concentrations.
tips: Never step off the boardwalk
Thin crust over boiling water
Gas collects in hollows

sections.heading: Ashfall and what it does
body: Volcanic ash is abrasive glass rather than soft soot. It damages engines and air filters, blocks windscreen washers and makes roads slippery, and it is a genuine respiratory irritant. Even light ashfall can close roads and airports at short notice.

If ashfall occurs, stay indoors or in the vehicle with vents closed, wear a proper mask rather than a cloth one if you must be outside, and do not drive unless necessary. Wetting ash before removing it stops it becoming airborne again.

sections.heading: Understanding the risk honestly
body: New Zealand's active volcanoes are closely monitored and the alert system is genuinely informative, but eruptions here have occurred with little or no useful warning. Whakaari in 2019 and Te Maari in 2012 both showed that unrest levels do not reliably predict short-term events.

That does not mean avoiding the central plateau. It means treating access restrictions as absolute, staying within signed areas, and accepting that a track closure is not a formality to be worked around.

Ruapehu also carries lahar risk in valleys draining the crater lake, which is why signage tells you not to linger in stream beds. Crossing quickly rather than stopping for a photograph is the entire requirement.

sections.heading: Travel disruption from ash
body: Ash closes airspace quickly and flights can be grounded for days, which matters more to most travellers than direct volcanic hazard. A significant Ruapehu or Taranaki event would disrupt domestic aviation across the country.
Keep a buffer before an international departure and travel insurance that covers natural disaster disruption. Neither is expensive and both are the practical response to volcanic risk here.
tips: Ash closes airspace for days
Buffer before international flights
Check insurance covers disruption

faq: Is it safe to camp near New Zealand's volcanoes?

Generally yes, at the normal alert levels, and Tongariro and Ruapehu are among the most visited places in the country. GeoNet publishes the alert level for each volcano, and access restrictions follow it.
What do the volcanic alert levels mean for a trip?

Level 0 to 2 covers everything from dormant to minor unrest, with tracks usually open and closer approaches sometimes restricted. From level 3 upward, eruption is under way and exclusion zones are enforced, which can close roads and huts at short notice.

river-crossing-safety-new-zealand.title: River Crossing Safety NZ: When to Cross and When Not
river-crossing-safety-new-zealand.description: New Zealand rivers rise fast after rain. How to judge a crossing, when to wait it out, and why turning back is the usual right answer.
river-crossing-safety-new-zealand.imageAlt: Fast New Zealand river crossing a backcountry route
river-crossing-safety-new-zealand.intro: Rivers cause serious backcountry incidents because depth, speed and bed stability are hard to judge from the bank. A planned turnaround point is more valuable than a memorised crossing manoeuvre.

sections.heading: Assess before entering
body: Check the forecast, recent rain and route advice before departure. Look for rising or discoloured water, moving debris, a strong current and no safe exit.
If the river is in flood, wait or turn back. Do not enter to test the depth and never cross merely because another group has started.

sections.heading: Use expertise honestly
body: River-crossing skills require practical instruction and good group judgement. Unbuckle pack straps where trained guidance recommends it and avoid linking up in ways the group has not practised.
Choose bridges or marked alternatives when available. A longer route is the correct route when the ford is doubtful.

sections.heading: Vehicle fords are hazards too
body: Know the manufacturer's wading limits and the road authority's closure status. Water can hide washouts and push a vehicle sideways at surprisingly low depth.
Never drive around a flood barrier. Park well back, wait for official reopening and keep enough food and fuel for the delay.

sections.heading: River crossings kill trampers here every year
body: New Zealand rivers rise fast, run cold and carry more force than they appear to. Drowning during crossings has historically been common enough to be described as the New Zealand death, and almost all of it involves people who decided to cross when they should have waited.
The decision is the skill. Turning back or waiting is always available and always safe; the crossing is not. If there is any doubt, there is no doubt.
tips: If in doubt, do not cross
Waiting is always the safe option
Most incidents are decision failures

sections.heading: Reading whether it is crossable
body: Look for a wide, straight, shallow reach with an even bed and a safe run-out below rather than rapids, logjams or a deep pool. Discoloured water, debris moving downstream, a rumbling sound of boulders and water above knee height on the shortest party member are all reasons not to cross.
Never cross where you cannot see the bottom, and never immediately above a hazard. Rivers change with every flood, so a crossing point described in an old guide may no longer exist.

sections.heading: If you do cross
body: Undo the waist belt and chest strap on your pack so it can be shed, keep boots on for grip, and face upstream slightly while moving across and downstream at an angle. Move one foot at a time and keep both feet planted before shifting weight.

Cross as a linked group where possible, with the strongest members on the upstream and downstream ends, and move together. If someone is swept away, they should go feet first on their back and swim for the bank at an angle rather than fighting the current.
tips: Undo pack straps before entering
Link up and move together
Feet first on your back if swept

sections.heading: Wait it out
body: Most New Zealand rivers drop as quickly as they rise, frequently within hours of the rain stopping. Carrying an extra day of food turns a dangerous decision into an inconvenient wait, which is why the standard advice is to plan for one.
Tell someone your intentions before you go so an overdue party triggers a response, and carry a personal locator beacon on any route with crossings. Both are cheap compared with the alternative.

sections.heading: Alternatives to crossing
body: Check whether a bridge exists upstream or downstream before committing, because many tracks have one within a reasonable distance and the detour is almost always shorter than the consequences of getting a crossing wrong.

Many New Zealand backcountry routes are unbridged by design, and the route description usually says whether crossings are expected. Where it does, treat that as a requirement for the skills and the willingness to wait rather than as a passing note.

Waiting is the most underused option available. Most rivers here drop within hours of the rain stopping, and carrying an extra day of food converts a dangerous decision into an inconvenient afternoon.

sections.heading: Learning before you need it
body: River crossing is a taught skill and reading about it is not the same as having practised. Outdoor clubs, guiding companies and some DOC visitor centres run or can point you towards training, and it is worth doing before a trip with crossings on it.
If nobody in the party has crossed a river before, choose a route that does not require it. There are plenty of excellent multi-day walks in New Zealand with bridged crossings throughout.
tips: Crossing is a taught skill
Choose bridged routes if untrained
Reading about it is not practice

faq: When is a New Zealand river unsafe to cross?

If it is discoloured, you cannot see the bottom, you can hear boulders moving, or the water is above the knees and pushing. River crossings are one of the most common causes of death in the New Zealand backcountry and the decision is almost always to wait.
How long do you have to wait for a flooded river to drop?

Often only hours. Most New Zealand rivers rise and fall quickly after rain, so an overnight wait usually solves it, which is why the huts are stocked for it and why turning back is a normal outcome rather than a failure.

winter-driving-new-zealand-campervan.title: Winter driving in a New Zealand campervan
winter-driving-new-zealand-campervan.description: Snow chains, black ice, wind and a high-sided vehicle require slower days and practised equipment.
winter-driving-new-zealand-campervan.imageAlt: Campervan driving on a snowy New Zealand road
winter-driving-new-zealand-campervan.intro: A campervan carries more side area, weight and stopping distance than the car many visitors drive at home. Winter adds conditions that make a legal speed entirely unsuitable.

sections.heading: Check the whole route
body: Read Waka Kotahi road status, MetService warnings and local chain-control information before departure. Recheck at the last town where waiting is comfortable.
Passes can be open while shaded approaches remain icy. Delay the drive until light and temperature improve.

sections.heading: Know the chains
body: Carry chains that fit the driven wheels and practise installation before the trip. Follow signs and authority directions about when and where they are required.
Use a safe fitting area, gloves and a torch. Never stop in a live lane or at the exact point where every unprepared driver has already queued.

sections.heading: Drive the vehicle you have
body: Accelerate, steer and brake gently, increase following distance and use lower gears on descents. Strong crosswinds can require a delay even without snow.
If confidence or visibility fails, turn back or use a legal stop. Rental schedules and prepaid camps do not reduce the physics.

sections.heading: Chains: carry, know, practise
body: Chain fitting is required at times on the Milford road, the Crown Range, the Lindis, Arthur's Pass, the Desert Road and others, and some rental agreements require you to carry them for the whole winter trip regardless of route. Enforcement at control points is real.

Fit them once at home, in daylight, on dry ground, so the first attempt is not in sleet on a narrow shoulder with traffic going past. That first attempt in bad conditions is where people give up and press on unequipped instead.
tips: Practise fitting in the dry first
Some rentals require carrying them always
Control points do enforce

sections.heading: Black ice
body: Black ice forms where the road merely looks wet, particularly in shade, on bridges and in the first and last hours of daylight. It gives no warning and no grip, and the instinctive responses of braking hard or steering sharply are both wrong.

Slow down before shaded sections rather than in them, increase following distance well beyond your summer habit, and if you do feel the vehicle go light, come off the accelerator gently and steer where you want to go without sudden input.

sections.heading: A campervan handles differently in winter
body: A high-sided vehicle is affected by crosswind far more than a car, and on a wet or icy road that combination is the one that puts vehicles off the edge. Its braking distance is longer, its centre of gravity higher, and it is heavier than it feels.

Slow down well before corners rather than during them, avoid sudden steering, and treat the posted limit as a maximum for perfect conditions rather than a target. Check tyre tread and pressures before the trip, because winter finds a marginal tyre quickly.
tips: Crosswind affects high-sided vans badly
Brake before the corner, not in it
Check tread and pressures before leaving

sections.heading: Shorter days, shorter plans
body: Midwinter gives roughly nine hours of usable light in the south, and a valley loses the sun well before official sunset. Driving legs that work in February become uncomfortable and then unsafe in July, so plan shorter days rather than earlier starts in the dark.

Check NZTA road conditions each morning, and treat a closure as a reason to reroute or stop rather than to wait indefinitely. Carry extra food, water, warm layers and charge, because a closure can hold you for hours.

sections.heading: Before you set out each morning
body: Check road conditions for every pass on the day's route on the morning itself, because closures and chain requirements are decided early. Then check the forecast for the pass rather than for the towns at either end, which can be completely different.
Clear all snow and ice off the vehicle including the roof before moving. Snow sliding off a roof onto your own windscreen at speed is a real hazard, and so is it landing on the vehicle behind you.

Refuel at half a tank rather than a quarter in winter. A closure can hold you for hours with the engine running for heat, and being low on fuel while stationary in the cold is a genuinely poor position to be in.

sections.heading: Where to stay in winter
body: Many DOC campsites close or turn off water over winter and small-town holiday parks reduce hours. Powered sites become considerably more valuable when you need heating overnight, and they book up around ski fields.
Base yourself in a town rather than remote sites when the forecast is poor. Being able to walk to food and warmth changes a bad-weather day from an ordeal into an ordinary one.
tips: Many DOC sites close for winter
Powered sites matter more in cold
Ski town parks book out

faq: Do you need snow chains in New Zealand?

On the alpine passes and access roads in winter, yes, and on some roads they are a legal requirement to proceed. Rental campervans usually carry them, and knowing how to fit them in the dark is the part people skip.
Which New Zealand roads close in winter?

The alpine passes and ski access roads are the ones that close or go chain-only, particularly the Crown Range, the Lindis, Arthur's Pass, the Desert Road and the Milford road. NZTA publishes live status and it changes through the day.
