new-zealand-road-signs-visitors.title: NZ Road Signs and Their Meanings for Visitors
new-zealand-road-signs-visitors.description: Give-way, one-lane bridge, advisory speed and warning signs in New Zealand explained, with the situations that catch visitors out on rural roads.
new-zealand-road-signs-visitors.imageAlt: New Zealand one-lane bridge warning sign
new-zealand-road-signs-visitors.intro: New Zealand signs use familiar international ideas but local road situations can surprise visitors. One-lane bridge priority, advisory corner speeds and temporary controls need recognition before the road narrows.

sections.heading: Limits and advisory numbers
body: A red-ring speed sign sets the maximum legal speed; a yellow advisory number indicates a safer corner speed rather than a new limit. Conditions can require travelling below both.
Temporary orange signs and portable limits are enforceable where installed. Continue obeying them until the end of the work zone.

sections.heading: One-lane bridges
body: A red-bordered give-way sign means traffic from your direction must yield. A blue rectangular priority sign gives your direction priority, but only when the bridge is clear and safe to enter.
Check for long or heavy vehicles already committed and never race another driver to the entrance.

sections.heading: Rail and rural hazards
body: Stop or give way at railway controls as signed, look both ways and never queue across tracks. Rural warning signs also identify stock, slips, ice and winding roads.
Learn the official visitor-driving material before collecting a rental. Navigation prompts do not explain the meaning of a roadside instruction.

sections.heading: Give Way rules at intersections
body: New Zealand's give way rules changed in 2012 and older overseas guidance is wrong. The current position is that at an uncontrolled intersection or when both vehicles face the same control, a turning vehicle gives way to a vehicle going straight through or turning left.

Roundabouts run clockwise and you give way to traffic on your right. Signal left as you leave, and take particular care on multi-lane roundabouts where lane markings determine which exit you may take.
tips: Turning gives way to straight-through
Roundabouts run clockwise
Give way to your right

sections.heading: One-lane bridge signage
body: One-lane bridges are common, particularly on the West Coast and in Northland. The sign shows two arrows: the larger black arrow indicates the direction with priority. If your arrow is the smaller red one, you give way to oncoming traffic.

Some bridges are shared with rail, and a few are long enough to include passing bays. Slow on approach, look right through the bridge before entering, and be willing to wait rather than racing to claim it.

sections.heading: Advisory speeds and hazard warnings
body: Yellow diamond signs are warnings rather than legal limits, and the yellow speed shown on a corner is an advisory maximum for a car in good conditions. In a loaded campervan, in rain, or towing, the safe speed is lower than the advisory figure.
Watch for the signs specific to New Zealand conditions: slippery when wet, loose metal, ford, stock crossing and the falling rocks warning used widely on the West Coast and through the passes.
tips: Yellow signs are advisory, not legal
Advisory speeds assume a car in the dry
Loose metal means gravel

sections.heading: Passing lanes and slow vehicle bays
body: Passing lanes are infrequent on New Zealand highways, and the courteous and expected behaviour if you are slower than the traffic behind is to use the slow vehicle bay or pull over where safe and let them pass. This is more than politeness; frustrated following drivers cause overtaking crashes.
Do not accelerate in a passing lane when someone is overtaking you. If your speed is holding up traffic, the road rules require you to move left and let it pass as soon as it is safe to do so.

sections.heading: Signs specific to New Zealand
body: LSZ marks a Limited Speed Zone on some rural roads, where the limit drops when conditions require it. A Ford sign means the road crosses a watercourse, which may be dry or impassable depending on recent rain.

Stock crossing and stock effluent signs indicate active farming use of the road. Slippery when wet appears widely on sealed rural roads where the chip seal becomes genuinely slick, and it is worth taking seriously in a heavy vehicle.

Blue and white signs mark tourist routes and services while brown signs indicate historic and cultural sites. Neither implies the road beyond is suitable for a large vehicle, so check that separately before turning off.

sections.heading: Roadworks and stop-go
body: Temporary works are frequent, particularly after winter damage, and a stop-go operator directing traffic has legal authority. Wait for the signal rather than following the vehicle in front through a closing gap.
Temporary limits apply whether or not work is visibly happening, including overnight and at weekends. The surface through works is often loose chip, which is genuinely slippery for a heavy vehicle.
tips: Stop-go operators have legal authority
Temporary limits apply at all hours
Loose chip is slippery

faq: Are New Zealand road signs different from other countries?

The shapes and colours will feel familiar, but the ones that catch visitors out are local: one-lane bridge priority arrows, the LSZ limited speed zone, and the yellow warning signs for gravel changes and stock crossings.
What does the one-lane bridge sign mean?

The large arrow is your direction and the small arrow is the oncoming one. If your arrow is the small one, you give way, and on a long bridge that means waiting at the entrance rather than committing and reversing.

overseas-driver-licence-new-zealand.title: Overseas Licence NZ 2026: Time Limit and Campervan Rules
overseas-driver-licence-new-zealand.description: Arrive by 31 October 2026 and an overseas car licence lasts 18 months; arrive later and it is 12. Translations, IDPs and the 6,000 kg campervan limit.
overseas-driver-licence-new-zealand.imageAlt: Visitor checking an overseas licence beside a campervan
overseas-driver-licence-new-zealand.intro: A current overseas car licence lets you drive in New Zealand for 18 months from your last arrival if you arrived between 1 November 2024 and 31 October 2026, and for 12 months if you arrive on or after 1 November 2026. It must be in English or come with an approved translation or International Driving Permit, and as a car licence it covers vehicles up to 6,000 kg, which takes in most rental campervans. Your home licence conditions still apply, and the rental company can add its own.

sections.heading: Current 2026 time limits
body: The limit depends on when you last arrived. A temporary rule from 1 November 2024 extended overseas car licences from 12 to 18 months, and it ends for new arrivals on 1 November 2026. If you arrived between 1 November 2024 and 31 October 2026, you keep 18 months from that arrival for as long as you stay in New Zealand. If you arrive on or after 1 November 2026, you get 12 months.

The extension only ever applied to car licences: overseas motorcycle and heavy-vehicle licences allow 12 months. The period runs from your most recent arrival, so leaving and re-entering starts it again, but the licence itself must stay current the whole time.

sections.heading: Translation and documents
body: A licence not in English needs an accurate approved translation or qualifying International Driving Permit, carried with the original current licence.
An IDP supports the original licence; it does not revive an expired, suspended or invalid document.

sections.heading: Vehicle class and conditions
body: A full overseas car licence generally aligns with New Zealand Class 1 up to 6,000 kg gross laden weight, subject to any lower home-licence limit. Larger motorhomes can require a different class.
Rental acceptance and insurance do not override licensing law. Confirm legal authority, contract and cover separately.

sections.heading: What you can drive on and for how long
body: You may drive on a current overseas licence for the period that applies to you, 18 or 12 months from your last arrival, provided the licence is valid, you have not been disqualified, and you drive only the vehicle classes it covers. After that you need a New Zealand licence.

Police can ask to see your licence whenever you drive, so carry the original licence every time, with the translation or IDP alongside it if it is not in English. An IDP supports the original and does not replace it.
tips: 18 months if you arrived by 31 October 2026
12 months if you arrive from 1 November 2026
Carry the original licence, not just an IDP

sections.heading: Can you drive a campervan on a car licence?
body: Usually, yes. A New Zealand car licence (Class 1) covers vehicles up to 6,000 kg gross laden weight, which is more generous than several other countries and covers most rental campervans and motorhomes. Larger motorhomes may fall outside it, and your home licence class is what determines the equivalence.

Rental companies apply their own age and licence conditions on top of the law, frequently requiring a minimum age and a licence held for a minimum period. Permission from a rental company does not override licensing law, and licensing law does not override the rental terms.

sections.heading: Restrictions carried from your home licence
body: Any condition on your original licence applies here: corrective lenses, automatic transmission only, an alcohol interlock, or a restricted class. Driving outside those conditions is an offence, and it can void your insurance.

A restricted or probationary licence from another country generally carries its restrictions with it. If you are on a graduated licence at home, check what that means before assuming you can drive freely here.
tips: Home licence conditions still apply
Automatic-only means automatic-only
Graduated licences carry restrictions

sections.heading: Insurance and the excess
body: Third party injury is covered for everyone by ACC regardless of fault, which is unusual and means you cannot sue for personal injury from a crash. Vehicle damage is not covered by that, and rental excess amounts here are frequently high.

Read what the excess reduction actually covers, because windscreen, tyres, undercarriage, water damage and single-vehicle accidents are commonly excluded even from reduced-excess products. Those are also the most likely things to happen on New Zealand roads.

sections.heading: Converting to a New Zealand licence
body: Once your 18 or 12 months is up, you must convert. Drivers from a list of recognised countries can convert without sitting theory or practical tests, while others must pass both. The list changes, so check the current position rather than relying on secondhand information.

Conversion requires proof of identity, your overseas licence, an eyesight check and a fee, and is handled through a licensing agent. Allow time, because the process is not instant and driving on an expired entitlement is an offence.
If you are staying long term and your country is not recognised, start early. Practical test bookings in the main centres can be weeks away, so do not leave it to the last month.

sections.heading: Renting with an overseas licence
body: Rental companies impose their own conditions beyond the law: a minimum age, a licence held for a minimum period, and sometimes a young-driver surcharge. Some decline licences from particular countries or require an International Driving Permit regardless.
Confirm these when booking rather than at the counter. Arriving at a depot and being refused the vehicle is a genuinely difficult problem to solve at an airport.
tips: Minimum age and licence-held periods apply
Some companies require an IDP regardless
Confirm at booking, not at pickup

faq: Can you drive in New Zealand on a foreign licence?

Yes. If you arrived between 1 November 2024 and 31 October 2026, a current overseas car licence lasts 18 months from that arrival; if you arrive on or after 1 November 2026, it lasts 12 months. After that you need a New Zealand licence.
Do you need an International Driving Permit for New Zealand?

Only if your licence is not in English. Where it is not, you must carry either an accurate English translation from an NZTA-approved translator or an International Driving Permit alongside the original licence.

sources.label: NZTA: driving in New Zealand on an overseas licence

campervan-road-rules-new-zealand.title: Campervan Driving Rules NZ: Licence, Speed and Size (2026)
campervan-road-rules-new-zealand.description: Driving a campervan in New Zealand: what a car licence covers, speed limits, wind on exposed roads, ferry dimensions and the mistakes visitors make.
campervan-road-rules-new-zealand.imageAlt: Large campervan on a narrow New Zealand road
campervan-road-rules-new-zealand.intro: A campervan can be legal on a Class 1 licence and still feel completely different from a car. The handover should establish height, width, length, loaded weight and every road excluded by the rental agreement.

sections.heading: Measure before moving
body: Record the vehicle dimensions where the driver can see them. Roof vents, air-conditioning units, bike racks and rear overhang affect clearances and manoeuvring.
All passengers need approved seats and restraints while travelling. Beds and rear living areas are not passenger positions unless certified as such.

sections.heading: Give the vehicle room
body: Brake earlier, take corners slowly and leave a larger following gap. Use mirrors deliberately and let following traffic pass at safe formed areas.
Strong crosswind can move a tall vehicle across the lane. Reduce speed or stop when steering corrections become constant.

sections.heading: Respect exclusions
body: Rental contracts may prohibit beaches, unsealed roads or named remote routes even when public access exists. Insurance can depend on the same conditions.
Stop before a low branch, weight-restricted bridge or uncertain ford. Vehicle recovery is not a substitute for clearance.

sections.heading: Know your dimensions before you drive off
body: Write down the height, length and weight of the vehicle and keep it where the driver can see it. Height is the one that causes expensive damage, on car park entrances, drive-throughs, service station canopies and a number of urban underpasses.
Check the mirrors, blind spots and reversing camera before leaving the depot, and walk the vehicle. Much rental campervan damage happens at low speed, in car parks.
tips: Write the height on the dashboard
Most damage happens in car parks
Walk the vehicle before you leave

sections.heading: Everyone travels in a proper seat
body: Beds, dinettes without belts and living areas are not passenger positions while the vehicle is moving. Every occupant needs an approved seat with a working belt, and child restraints are required for under-sevens with specific standards applying.
Secure everything loose before every drive. A cupboard door, a gas bottle or a full kettle becomes dangerous under emergency braking, and campervans brake later and harder than a car.

sections.heading: Wind, and why it matters more here
body: A high-sided vehicle catches crosswind badly, and New Zealand is a windy country with exposed coastal roads, bridges and mountain gaps. Overtaking trucks and emerging from cuttings both produce sudden lateral shoves.

Hold the wheel firmly with both hands in exposed sections, slow down before rather than during a gust, and check NZTA's journey planner before an exposed crossing: the Remutaka Hill Road (SH2) closes in severe wind, and other exposed roads carry wind cautions.
tips: Slow before the exposed section
Some roads close in severe wind
Trucks and cuttings cause sudden gusts

sections.heading: Overtaking and being overtaken
body: A campervan accelerates slowly, so overtaking requires far more clear road than a car needs and is rarely worth attempting. Most of New Zealand's highways are two-lane with limited passing lanes and a poor overtaking crash record.

When traffic builds behind you, pull over where safe and let it past. If you are holding up traffic, the road rules require you to move left and let it pass as soon as it is safe, and it also removes the pressure that causes people to overtake badly.

sections.heading: Parking and overnight legality
body: Parking a campervan is a different question from camping in it. A vehicle can be legally parked somewhere and still be prohibited from being occupied overnight, and that distinction is what most infringements actually turn on.

Height restrictions in urban car parks catch campervans out constantly, and the barrier is usually the first indication. Look for signed height limits before entering, and use the surface or overflow parking most towns provide for larger vehicles.
In cities the practical approach is to leave the vehicle at a campground or park-and-ride and take public transport in. It is faster, cheaper and avoids the entire problem rather than managing it.

sections.heading: Ferries, tunnels and height limits
body: Cook Strait vehicle fares are set by length, including bike racks and towbars, and length is checked at check-in. Some urban tunnels and older bridges carry height or weight restrictions, and a few exposed routes close in severe wind.
Know your dimensions precisely and check them against any route with a tunnel, a low bridge or a ferry booking. Guessing is what produces an expensive adjustment at a terminal or worse on a road.
tips: Ferry fares are set by size
Know exact height and length
Exposed routes can close in severe wind

faq: Are the speed limits different for a campervan?

For most rental campervans and motorhomes under 3,500 kg, no: the open road limit applies as normal. Heavier vehicles and anything towing are held to a lower limit, and the limit is a maximum rather than a target on a winding road.
What catches campervan drivers out in New Zealand?

Height and width on narrow roads, wind on exposed passes and bridges, and the habit of forming a queue behind you. Pulling over to let traffic past is expected here and is the single thing that most reduces the risk.

sources.label: NZTA driving on New Zealand roads

wof-registration-campervan-new-zealand.title: NZ Campervan WoF and Rego: What to Check Before You Drive
wof-registration-campervan-new-zealand.description: How a Warrant of Fitness and vehicle registration work for a campervan in New Zealand, how to check the expiry dates and what an expired WoF means.
wof-registration-campervan-new-zealand.imageAlt: New Zealand vehicle inspection and registration labels
wof-registration-campervan-new-zealand.intro: Light campervans generally need a current Warrant of Fitness and vehicle licence, while heavier or passenger-service vehicles can operate under different inspection systems. Check the exact vehicle rather than assuming the rental category answers it.

sections.heading: Read the labels
body: Confirm the inspection and licensing expiry dates before departure. A WoF checks specified safety items at the inspection date; it is not a guarantee against later mechanical failure.
Ask the operator to explain any Certificate of Fitness or road-user-charge display relevant to the vehicle.

sections.heading: Driver checks still matter
body: Inspect tyres, lights, mirrors, windscreen, fluids and warning lamps. Report damage before leaving the depot and photograph the agreed condition.
Secure cupboards, gas bottles, tables and loose gear. A legal vehicle can still become unsafe when the living space is not prepared for motion.

sections.heading: When something changes
body: Stop safely for a warning light, tyre issue or new vibration. Contact the rental or roadside provider before continuing in a way that may worsen damage.
Do not alter seats, plumbing, gas or structural fittings without qualified approval. Modifications can affect inspection, certification and insurance.

sections.heading: What a WoF actually covers
body: A Warrant of Fitness is a periodic safety inspection covering brakes, tyres, lights, steering, structure and glazing. It is a snapshot on the day of inspection rather than a guarantee of condition, and the legal responsibility to keep the vehicle roadworthy sits with the driver at all times.

Driving a vehicle with an expired WoF is an offence and can void insurance. Check the label on the windscreen when you collect a rental, and check that the expiry covers your entire hire period rather than just the pickup date.
tips: Check the expiry covers your whole hire
A WoF is a snapshot, not a guarantee
Expired WoF can void insurance

sections.heading: Registration and road user charges
body: Vehicle licensing, commonly called rego, must be current and is displayed on the windscreen. Diesel vehicles additionally require road user charges purchased in advance per thousand kilometres, and running past the distance purchased carries a penalty.

For a rental, ask whether RUC is included in the daily rate or billed separately at the end, because on a long trip in a diesel campervan it is a meaningful amount that can arrive as an unexpected charge.

sections.heading: Self-containment is a separate certificate
body: Self-containment certification is not part of a WoF and proves nothing about roadworthiness. Equally, a current WoF says nothing about whether a vehicle may be used for freedom camping. They are independent requirements and you may need both.
Check the self-containment warrant against the vehicle registration on the public register rather than trusting the sticker, and confirm the certified occupancy matches your party.
tips: WoF and self-containment are unrelated
Check the plate on the SCV register
Confirm certified occupancy

sections.heading: Checks worth doing yourself
body: Before a long leg, check tyre pressures and tread including the spare, the oil and coolant levels, the lights and the windscreen washers. Rental campervans are frequently handed over with underinflated tyres, which costs fuel and handling at once.

Confirm the spare, jack and wheel brace are actually present and that you know where the jacking points are. Discovering they are missing on a gravel road on the West Coast is a considerably worse time to find out.

sections.heading: If something goes wrong on the road
body: Rental agreements set out who to call and what you may arrange yourself. Getting repairs done without approval frequently voids reimbursement, so call first even when the fix seems obvious and the delay is irritating.

For a breakdown in a remote area, stay with the vehicle. It is shelter, it is far easier for rescuers to spot than a person walking, and on many South Island roads walking out is considerably worse than waiting.

Carry the roadside assistance number written down rather than only in a phone, and be able to describe where you are. A road name and the nearest identifiable landmark is usually enough for a tow operator to find you.

sections.heading: Returning the vehicle
body: Most disputes at return are about cleanliness, fuel level, tank emptying and undeclared damage. Photograph the vehicle inside and out at pickup and again at return, with the odometer and fuel gauge visible.
Empty and rinse the waste tanks before returning, because cleaning charges are high and easily avoided. Read what condition the agreement requires rather than assuming a reasonable standard.
tips: Photograph at pickup and return
Empty tanks before returning
Cleaning charges are steep

faq: What is a Warrant of Fitness and does it affect a rental?

It is New Zealand's periodic vehicle safety inspection, and every vehicle on the road needs a current one along with current registration. A rental company is responsible for both, but it is worth checking the labels on the windscreen before you drive away.
What should you check before driving a rental campervan away?

The WoF and registration labels, the self-containment certificate and its expiry, the tyres including the spare, and where the chains and the jack are. A self-containment certificate that expires mid-trip turns legal free camping into a fine.

towing-caravan-new-zealand.title: Towing a Caravan in NZ: Licence, Weight and 90 km/h Limit
towing-caravan-new-zealand.description: 90 km/h maximum with a towbar, 50 km/h on a rope, 6,000 kg combined on a full car licence, plus loading, sway and the roads to take slowly.
towing-caravan-new-zealand.imageAlt: Car towing a caravan on a New Zealand highway
towing-caravan-new-zealand.intro: A stable caravan depends on the legal combination, correct loading and a driver who slows before the road demands it. New Zealand's curves and wind make the maximum permitted speed irrelevant on many sections.

sections.heading: Know the combination
body: Check the tow rating, coupling, safety chain, lights, tyres, brakes and loaded weights for both vehicles. Account for water, gas, bikes and equipment added after the empty specification.
Passengers cannot travel inside a caravan on the road. Everyone belongs in an approved restrained seat in the tow vehicle.

sections.heading: Speed and spacing
body: The maximum open-road speed while towing is 90 km/h with a rigid connection such as a towbar. With a rope or other non-rigid connection the limit is 50 km/h on any road. Travel slower whenever stability, visibility, weather or the road requires it.
Leave at least a four-second gap, with more in bad weather. Brake before corners and select a lower gear for descents.

sections.heading: Share narrow roads
body: Use safe pull-over areas to let following traffic pass and approach one-lane bridges only when the full combination can clear.
Strong wind, trailer sway or hot brakes require a stop. Do not attempt to recover lost itinerary time by increasing speed.

sections.heading: Towing speed limits are lower
body: Light trailers and caravans are limited to 90 km/h on the open road, below the 100 km/h general limit, and heavy trailer combinations are also capped at 90 km/h. It is a maximum, not a target: where a lower limit is posted, the lower limit applies.
Leave a much larger following gap than you would in a car. Braking distance increases substantially with a trailer, especially on long descents.
tips: 90 km/h maximum when towing
Braking distance increases sharply
Bigger following gap than a car

sections.heading: Weights, ratings and loading
body: The tow vehicle's maximum towing capacity, the towbar rating, the caravan's gross laden weight and the tow ball download all have to agree, and the limiting figure is whichever is lowest. Exceeding any of them affects handling, braking and insurance.

Load heavy items low and over the axle, keep roughly ten percent of the weight on the tow ball, and avoid loading the rear of the caravan, which is what causes sway. Check the load again after the first hour of driving.

sections.heading: Sway and how to respond
body: Sway usually starts from a crosswind gust, a passing truck or too little tow ball weight, and it builds rather than settling. The instinct to brake hard or steer against it makes it worse.

Ease off the accelerator gently, keep the steering straight, and let the combination slow itself. If your vehicle has a trailer brake controller, applying the trailer brakes alone can pull the combination straight. Then stop and check the loading.
tips: Ease off, do not brake hard
Keep the steering straight
Stop and recheck the load after

sections.heading: Roads to think twice about
body: Tākaka Hill, the Crown Range, Remutaka Hill Road, the unsealed 309 Road and much of the Coromandel coast are steep, tight and slow with a caravan, and Remutaka Hill (SH2) closes in severe wind. Check road conditions and any restrictions before committing, since turning around is often not possible.

On descents, select a lower gear and use engine braking rather than riding the brakes, which fade. Pull over regularly to let following traffic past, both as courtesy and because a queue behind you creates overtaking risk.

sections.heading: Reversing, parking and campgrounds
body: Practise reversing in an empty car park before the trip. Campground sites frequently require a reverse into a defined space with neighbours close on both sides, and doing that for the first time with an audience is how people damage vans.
Book sites that suit your combination length and say you are towing when you book. Many holiday parks keep specific drive-through sites, and getting one removes most of the difficulty from arrival.

Unhitching gives you an ordinary vehicle for day trips and is worth doing whenever you stay more than one night. Use wheel chocks and levelling ramps, and check the handbrake holds before disconnecting anything.

sections.heading: Wind and exposed roads
body: A caravan is a large flat surface and crosswind is a major cause of sway and loss of control while towing. Exposed sections around Wellington, the Desert Road, the Mackenzie and coastal Canterbury are all known for it.
Slow down before exposed sections rather than reacting within them, and take particular care when emerging from a cutting or passing a truck, where the wind loads and unloads suddenly.
tips: Crosswind is the main towing hazard
Slow before exposed sections
Trucks cause sudden gusts

faq: What is the speed limit when towing in New Zealand?

90 km/h on the open road with a towbar or other rigid connection, below the 100 km/h general limit, and any lower posted limit still applies. With a rope or other non-rigid connection the limit is 50 km/h on any road.
Do you need a special licence to tow a caravan in New Zealand?

Not usually. A full car licence lets you tow when the vehicle, trailer and load together weigh no more than 6,000 kg; on a learner or restricted licence the limit is 4,500 kg. Rental agreements can set their own lower limits.

speed-limits-new-zealand-visitors.title: NZ Speed Limits 2026: Open Road 100 km/h, Towing 90
speed-limits-new-zealand-visitors.description: New Zealand speed limits for visitors and campervans: 100 km/h on the open road, 50 km/h in towns, 90 km/h when towing, and when to drive well below them.
speed-limits-new-zealand-visitors.imageAlt: New Zealand speed limit sign on a rural road
speed-limits-new-zealand-visitors.intro: A legal limit is not a promise that a road can be driven at that speed. Corners, rain, gravel, stock, cyclists and an unfamiliar campervan all reduce the safe pace.

sections.heading: Read each change
body: Speed limits vary by road and location, with temporary limits at works and lower zones around many communities or schools. Watch signs rather than relying on a remembered national default.
A yellow advisory speed before a corner is not the legal limit, but it communicates road geometry that deserves attention.

sections.heading: Slow before the hazard
body: Brake on the straight before entering a curve and keep enough margin to stop within the visible road. Gravel and wet leaves reduce grip well before a warning appears.
At night or in fog, reduce speed until the headlights reveal enough stopping distance. High beams cannot solve a winding road.

sections.heading: Do not create pressure
body: Let faster traffic pass at safe formed areas. Never speed up on a passing lane only to hold a queue again at the next bend.
If the planned arrival depends on driving at every posted maximum, the itinerary is already too tight.

sections.heading: The posted limit is a maximum, not a target
body: The open road limit is generally 100 km/h and urban areas are usually 50 km/h, with variable and reduced limits around schools, roadworks and some rural highways. The limit assumes ideal conditions, a car, and a driver familiar with the road.

Almost no New Zealand rural highway is comfortable at 100 km/h in a loaded campervan, in rain, or on an unfamiliar winding section. Driving at a speed that suits the conditions is both legal and expected, and driving too slowly on a straight is not the same thing as driving safely.
tips: 100 km/h open road, 50 urban
Limits assume ideal conditions
Towing is capped at 90 km/h

sections.heading: Enforcement is tighter than many visitors expect
body: The tolerance is small, speed cameras are widespread including mobile units, and fines are issued to the registered keeper, which means a rental company will pass them on with an administration fee. Offences where police stop you carry demerit points even on an overseas licence, and the fines apply too.
Average speed cameras have expanded since late 2025, so assume any road may be monitored. Assume any road may be monitored rather than looking for cameras.

sections.heading: Why the roads themselves demand less speed
body: New Zealand highways are largely two-lane, undivided, with tight radii, variable camber, one-lane bridges, unfenced stock and frequent unsealed side roads throwing gravel onto the surface. There is very little forgiving shoulder.

That combination is why crash rates involving visiting drivers are concentrated on rural roads. The safe pace is usually well below the limit, and the time lost across a day is a few minutes rather than the hour people imagine.
tips: Two-lane, undivided, little shoulder
Gravel gets thrown onto sealed roads
Driving slower costs minutes, not hours

sections.heading: Speed and the passing lane
body: Do not increase speed when a passing lane appears and someone is overtaking you. It is the most common source of conflict on New Zealand highways and it turns a safe overtake into a dangerous one.

Equally, if you are being followed closely, do not feel pressured to exceed a speed you are comfortable with. Use the next slow vehicle bay or safe pull-off and let them go; the pressure disappears and so does the risk.

sections.heading: Variable and reduced limits
body: Limits around schools drop at set times and are signed with flashing or variable displays. Roadworks carry temporary limits that apply whether or not anyone is visibly working, and they are enforced with the same small tolerance as permanent limits.

Some rural roads carry limits below 100 km/h, and many reduced limits were raised again in 2025, so an older map or a previous visit can be wrong in either direction. Read the signs rather than assuming the open road limit applies.

On unsealed roads the posted limit is frequently still 100 km/h, which is nowhere near a safe speed on gravel. Here the limit is genuinely a legal maximum rather than any indication of what the surface supports.

sections.heading: How speed cameras and fines work
body: Fixed and mobile cameras operate throughout the country and the enforcement tolerance is small. Fines are issued to the registered keeper, so a rental company receives them and passes them on with an administration fee.

Speed-camera fines carry no demerit points, but offences where police stop you do, even on an overseas licence; 100 points within two years means a three-month ban from driving in New Zealand. Pay them rather than assuming they disappear when you leave.
tips: Small enforcement tolerance
Rentals add an admin fee
Unpaid fines follow you

faq: What is the open road speed limit in New Zealand?
100 km/h unless signed otherwise, 50 km/h in urban areas, and 90 km/h if you are towing. Some highways are signed at 110 km/h and many rural roads are signed lower.
Why do New Zealand roads take longer than the distance suggests?
Because the posted limit is rarely achievable. The roads are narrow, winding and often single lane in each direction, so a realistic average is well under the limit and a 300 km day is a full day.

alcohol-fatigue-driving-new-zealand.title: Drink Driving Limit in New Zealand for Visitors (2026)
alcohol-fatigue-driving-new-zealand.description: Limit: 250 micrograms per litre of breath at 20 and over, zero under 20. What a checkpoint involves and why the first drive after a flight should be short.
alcohol-fatigue-driving-new-zealand.imageAlt: Driver resting beside a campervan before continuing
alcohol-fatigue-driving-new-zealand.intro: Visitors often combine a long flight, an unfamiliar vehicle and left-side driving on the same day. Treat rest as part of the booking and keep alcohol completely separate from any driving responsibility.

sections.heading: Rest after the flight
body: Book a nearby first night or use depot transport rather than starting a major drive jet-lagged. Learn controls, mirrors and vehicle size in daylight.
Fatigue signs include repeated yawning, wandering attention and missed signs. Stop at the first warning rather than bargaining for the next town.

sections.heading: Alcohol rules vary by driver
body: Drivers under 20 must have zero alcohol. Other legal limits and penalties do not establish a safe personal amount, especially with fatigue, medication or an unfamiliar road.
Nominate a sober driver or leave the vehicle parked. Coffee, food and a short wait do not rapidly remove alcohol.

sections.heading: Build real breaks
body: Change drivers where both are licensed and insured, stop for movement and avoid long night sections. Rest areas are for safe breaks, not automatically legal camping.
Plan the campsite before fatigue peaks. A booked nearby holiday park is cheaper than a crash, infringement or damaged vehicle.

sections.heading: The legal limits
body: For drivers aged 20 and over the limit is 250 micrograms of alcohol per litre of breath, or 50 milligrams per 100 millilitres of blood. For drivers under 20 the limit is zero. Both are enforced through frequent checkpoints, including on rural roads and during the day.

There is no reliable way to estimate your own level, and the standard drink calculations circulating online do not account for body composition, food, fatigue or the previous evening. The only safe approach on a road trip is to separate drinking from driving completely.
tips: Zero limit under 20
250 mcg breath, 50 mg blood over 20
Checkpoints are common and random

sections.heading: Morning-after driving
body: This is where visitors most often get caught. Alcohol clears at roughly one standard drink an hour and no faster, so a heavy evening can leave you over the limit well into the following morning. Sleep, coffee and a shower do nothing to speed it up.

On a camping trip the vehicle is right there and the temptation to move early is strong. If you drank substantially, plan to leave late rather than early, and build that into the itinerary rather than deciding at 7am.

sections.heading: Fatigue is the larger risk on this trip
body: Long-haul flight arrival, jet lag, an unfamiliar vehicle, driving on the other side and winding roads combine badly, and the long, winding stretches between towns leave little margin for a tired driver. Keep the first driving day short, before your body clock has caught up.
Do not collect a campervan and drive for four hours on arrival day. Stay near the airport the first night, take the first driving day short, and swap drivers regularly if you can.
tips: Do not drive far on arrival day
Keep the first driving day short
Swap drivers every two hours

sections.heading: Recognising it before it matters
body: Yawning, heavy eyes, drifting in the lane, missing a turn, and having no memory of the last few kilometres are all late signs rather than early ones. By the time you notice them, reaction time is already substantially impaired.

Stop every two hours as a rule rather than when you feel tired. A twenty minute nap is genuinely effective; music, fresh air, energy drinks and conversation are not, and they mainly mask the symptoms while the impairment continues.

sections.heading: Planning a trip that avoids the problem
body: Build wine region visits around a designated driver, a bicycle or a tour rather than intending to be careful. Marlborough, Hawke's Bay, Central Otago and Martinborough are all compact enough that cycling between cellar doors is the normal approach.
Where you plan to drink, plan to stay. Booking the campground at the place you are drinking rather than half an hour away removes the decision entirely, and it usually costs the same.

On fatigue, build the itinerary so no day needs more than about four hours of driving, and put the shortest day immediately after your international arrival. Most fatigue problems here are itinerary problems rather than willpower problems.

sections.heading: What a checkpoint involves
body: Police can stop any vehicle and require a breath screening test without suspecting anything. Checkpoints appear on rural roads and at all hours, not only late at night near cities.

The screening test takes seconds. If you fail it, or do not or cannot complete it, police can require an evidential breath test or a blood test, and refusing a required blood test is an offence carrying penalties like those for drink driving. There is nothing to gain from declining.
tips: Any vehicle can be stopped
Checkpoints run at all hours
Refusing a blood test is an offence

faq: What is the drink-driving limit in New Zealand?

250 micrograms of alcohol per litre of breath for drivers aged 20 and over, which is a blood alcohol limit of 0.05. For drivers under 20 the limit is zero, and enforcement is by frequent random breath testing.
Why is fatigue such a risk on New Zealand road trips?

Because the driving demands constant attention and the distances feel shorter than they drive. Long-haul flight arrivals, an unfamiliar side of the road and a winding highway combine badly, which is why the first day is the one to keep short.

left-side-driving-new-zealand.title: Driving on the Left in New Zealand: First-Day Guide
left-side-driving-new-zealand.description: New Zealand drives on the left. How roundabouts and the 2012 give-way rules work, and how to keep old habits away on a first day in a campervan.
left-side-driving-new-zealand.imageAlt: Left-side driving view on a New Zealand road
left-side-driving-new-zealand.intro: Remembering the left is easiest in flowing traffic and hardest after a stop, on an empty road or while turning. Create simple checks that survive distraction and tiredness.

sections.heading: Set up the cockpit
body: Adjust mirrors, seat and navigation before moving. Place a small legal reminder where the driver can see it without obstructing the windscreen.
The driver should remain near the centre line and the passenger side near the road edge. Use lane markings rather than copying another vehicle blindly.

sections.heading: Slow the decision points
body: Pause at every turn and look in both directions, then enter the left lane. At roundabouts, give way according to New Zealand rules and signal the intended exit.
Take extra care when restarting from a scenic stop or petrol station, where no traffic may reveal the correct side.

sections.heading: Reset without panic
body: If orientation feels wrong, slow smoothly and stop in a legal safe place. Do not swerve across lanes or reverse into traffic.
Share driving only with people who are licensed, rested and covered by the rental agreement. The first practice session belongs in daylight.

sections.heading: The moments it goes wrong
body: Experienced drivers do not drift to the wrong side while cruising; they get it wrong at specific moments. Pulling out of a car park or driveway, turning at a quiet intersection, setting off after a rest stop, and the first turn after a distraction are where it happens.

Build a deliberate habit for those moments: say it out loud, look for the centre line on your right, and check the passenger side is nearest the kerb. The driver sits on the right, so if the kerb is on your side, you are on the wrong side of the road.
tips: Driver sits right, kerb on the left
Errors happen at turns and after stops
Say it out loud at every pull-out

sections.heading: Set the vehicle up before you move
body: Adjust the mirrors, seat and navigation before leaving the depot, not while driving. The indicator and wiper stalks are often reversed from what you are used to, and using the wipers instead of the indicator at a junction is the classic first-day mistake.
Practise in the car park first: a few laps, a reverse, and a couple of turns. Ten minutes there is worth an hour of unlearning on a live road.

sections.heading: Judging the width and the left side
body: Sitting on the right means your sense of where the left edge of the vehicle sits is wrong, and drivers new to the left commonly clip kerbs and drift towards the verge. In a campervan that verge is often unsealed with a soft drop.
Use the lane markings rather than instinct, and position with the centre line at a consistent distance from your right shoulder. If you are clipping the left, you are further left than you think.
tips: You will misjudge the left edge
Position off the centre line
Verges are soft and drop away

sections.heading: Roundabouts and give way
body: Roundabouts run clockwise and you give way to your right, which is the opposite of what a right-side driver expects. Approach slowly, look right, and do not commit until you are certain. Multi-lane roundabouts require the correct lane on entry, marked on the road.

At intersections, a vehicle that is turning gives way to one going straight through, a long-standing rule. Two changes from 25 March 2012 are the ones visitors miss: if you are turning right, you give way to oncoming traffic turning left, and at a T-intersection traffic on the road that ends gives way to all traffic on the road that continues. Guides written before 2012 describe the old right-turn rule, so ignore them.

sections.heading: The first day
body: Do not collect a vehicle and immediately drive a long distance, particularly straight off a long-haul flight. Book somewhere near the pickup point for the first night and keep the first driving day short and on main roads rather than winding rural ones.
Have a passenger act as a second pair of eyes for the first few days, specifically calling out turns and pull-outs. It feels excessive and it prevents exactly the error that causes head-on crashes.

Expect the concentration required to be tiring. Driving on the other side is genuinely more demanding until it becomes automatic, usually after two or three days, so build in more breaks than you normally would.

sections.heading: Overtaking from the left-hand side
body: Overtaking requires pulling into the oncoming lane on your right, which feels wrong at first and needs a longer clear stretch than you would use at home because your sightline from the right-hand seat is different.
Most New Zealand highways are two-lane with few passing lanes. If overtaking feels marginal, do not; arriving five minutes later is a trade nobody has ever regretted.
tips: Overtake to the right
Sightlines differ from the right seat
If it feels marginal, do not

faq: Which side of the road does New Zealand drive on?
The left, with the driver on the right of the vehicle. The turns that catch people out are the ones made from a standing start, particularly pulling out of a car park or a rural driveway.
What is the hardest part of switching to driving on the left?

Not the open road, which settles within an hour, but intersections, roundabouts taken clockwise, and the moment after a stop when the habit reasserts itself. A note on the dashboard and a passenger who calls it out both help more than they sound like they would.

sources.label: NZTA driving on New Zealand roads

one-lane-bridges-gravel-roads-new-zealan.title: One-lane bridges and gravel roads in New Zealand
one-lane-bridges-gravel-roads-new-zealan.description: Priority signs, dust and loose surfaces need calm decisions from larger vehicles.
one-lane-bridges-gravel-roads-new-zealan.imageAlt: One-lane bridge on a remote New Zealand road
one-lane-bridges-gravel-roads-new-zealan.intro: Rural roads can narrow from a centre line to one bridge deck without much transition. Read the priority sign early, slow on the straight and assume the next vehicle may be larger than it first appears.

sections.heading: Give way correctly
body: The round red sign indicates that your direction gives way; the blue rectangular sign indicates priority. Priority still requires the bridge to be clear and safe.
Wait well back so an oncoming truck or caravan has room to leave the bridge. Never stop on railway tracks incorporated into a bridge.

sections.heading: Adapt to gravel
body: Reduce speed before the loose surface, increase following distance and avoid abrupt steering or braking. Dust can hide vehicles, cyclists and livestock.
Slow significantly for oncoming traffic to reduce stone damage and maintain control near the edge.

sections.heading: Check the contract
body: Public access does not guarantee that a rental permits the road. Review unsealed-road exclusions and named prohibited routes before leaving the highway.
Turn back at washouts, deep fords or no-exit roads without turning room. A map line is not evidence of current vehicle access.

sections.heading: Reading a one-lane bridge sign
body: The sign carries two arrows. The large black arrow shows the direction with priority; the small red arrow means you give way. If the red arrow points your way, stop and wait for oncoming traffic to clear before entering.

Slow on approach regardless of who has priority, and look right through the bridge to the far end before committing. Some are long enough that a vehicle can already be on it and not yet visible, and a few include a passing bay mid-span.
tips: Large black arrow has priority
Look through to the far end first
Slow down even when you have right of way

sections.heading: Bridges shared with rail
body: A number of one-lane bridges, particularly on the West Coast, carry a railway line down the middle or alongside the traffic lane. Trains always have priority and the signage and lights must be obeyed absolutely.
Do not stop on these bridges for photographs, and do not enter if lights are flashing. The clearances are tight and there is nowhere to go if you have misjudged it.

sections.heading: Driving gravel properly
body: Reduce speed well below what feels necessary; most gravel crashes happen because the driver was travelling at sealed-road speed. Brake and steer gently and separately, avoid sudden inputs, and expect the vehicle to move around under you, particularly in a corrugated section.

Pull over and slow right down for oncoming vehicles to reduce stone damage to both, and leave a very large gap behind anything throwing dust, because visibility can go to nothing. Windscreen chips are the most common rental damage claim on these roads.
tips: Slow well below sealed-road speed
Gentle, separate braking and steering
Huge gap behind anything raising dust

sections.heading: Check your rental agreement first
body: Most rental agreements prohibit specific unsealed roads by name and some exclude gravel entirely, with damage on them not covered. Skippers Canyon, Ninety Mile Beach and several others are commonly named exclusions, and the vehicle is tracked.

Read the agreement before planning a route that includes gravel, and be aware that a road being open and legal does not mean your insurance follows you onto it. When in doubt, take the sealed alternative.

sections.heading: Punctures and windscreen damage
body: Stone chips are the most common damage on unsealed roads and many excess reduction products exclude glass. Check whether yours does before driving gravel, and consider the separate windscreen cover most operators offer, which is usually inexpensive.

For a puncture, get well off the road before jacking, because a vehicle on a soft or sloping gravel shoulder is genuinely dangerous. Confirm the spare, jack and brace exist and that you know the jacking points before the trip rather than during it.
On a remote gravel road with no reception, staying with the vehicle is the right call. It is shelter, it is visible, and somebody will pass eventually on almost any road that appears on a map.

sections.heading: Dust and following distance
body: Dust from a vehicle ahead can reduce visibility to nothing within seconds, and it hides oncoming traffic, corners and stock. This is the most underestimated hazard on New Zealand gravel.
Drop well back rather than pushing through, and put headlights on so others can see you. If you cannot see the road, slow to walking pace or stop somewhere visible until it clears.
tips: Dust hides oncoming traffic
Drop right back, do not push through
Headlights on for gravel

faq: How do one-lane bridges work in New Zealand?

The sign shows two arrows, and the larger one is the direction with priority. If the small arrow is yours you give way, and you wait at the entrance rather than starting across and meeting someone in the middle.
How should you drive on New Zealand gravel roads?

Slower than feels necessary, with more following distance and no sudden steering or braking. Most rental agreements exclude some gravel roads entirely, so it is worth reading that before taking a shortcut.

wildlife-livestock-road-safety-new-zeala.title: Wildlife, livestock and rural road safety
wildlife-livestock-road-safety-new-zeala.description: Sheep, seals, birds and farm vehicles can enter the road where a visitor expects an empty lane.
wildlife-livestock-road-safety-new-zeala.imageAlt: Sheep beside a rural New Zealand road
wildlife-livestock-road-safety-new-zeala.intro: New Zealand roads pass working farms and wildlife habitat at close range. Speed and distance are the only reliable tools when an animal behaves unpredictably.

sections.heading: Expect stock
body: Slow well before sheep, cattle, horses or a farmer controlling movement. Follow gestures and never sound the horn aggressively through a mob.
Manure, mud and wet grass can reduce grip after the animals pass. Accelerate gently and give farm vehicles room.

sections.heading: Protect coastal wildlife
body: At seal and penguin areas, park only in formed spaces and walk the final distance. Keep the legal or advised separation and never stand between an animal and the sea.
Birds may nest beside roads or strike vehicles at dusk. Lower speed around signed habitat and avoid night driving through active areas.

sections.heading: After a collision
body: Stop safely, protect people from traffic and call 111 for an emergency. Report stock or injured protected wildlife to the responsible authority.
Do not handle an injured wild animal without direction. Stress, teeth and traffic can create another casualty.

sections.heading: Stock on the road is normal here
body: Herds being moved between paddocks on rural roads are routine, and you may come around a corner into a full dairy herd. Slow right down, stop if asked, and follow the directions of the farmer or the person moving them.
Move through slowly and steadily rather than trying to weave; the animals will part around a slow vehicle. Do not sound the horn, which scatters stock and makes it considerably worse for everyone.
tips: Stop and follow the farmer's directions
Move slowly, do not weave
Never use the horn near stock

sections.heading: Unfenced roads and wandering animals
body: Many rural and high country roads are unfenced, and sheep, cattle and deer can be on the carriageway at any time, day or night. This is particularly common in the Mackenzie, Central Otago, Northland and on back roads everywhere.
At night, animals appear at the edge of your headlights with very little warning. Reduce speed on unfenced roads after dark, and be aware that where there is one animal there are usually more.

sections.heading: Do not swerve
body: Braking in a straight line is almost always the correct response to an animal on the road. Swerving is what turns an animal strike into a rollover, a head-on or a departure off the road, and in a high-sided campervan the rollover risk is real.
Possums, hares and rabbits are the most common animals hit and are not worth any evasive action at all. For larger stock, brake hard and straight and accept the impact rather than leaving the road.
tips: Brake straight, never swerve
Swerving causes rollovers
Possums are not worth evasive action

sections.heading: Protected wildlife on and near roads
body: Kea at Arthur's Pass, Homer Tunnel and Fiordland car parks are drawn to vehicles and are regularly killed on roads. Penguins cross roads near the coast in Oamaru, the Catlins and Banks Peninsula, and blue penguins nest under buildings and vehicles.

Never feed kea, which is what brought them to car parks in the first place. Check under and around a parked vehicle before moving it in penguin areas, and drive slowly through signed wildlife zones after dark.

sections.heading: Rural driving beyond the animals
body: Farm vehicles, tractors and stock trucks use rural roads at low speed and turn into unmarked gateways with little warning. Expect mud on the road near farm entrances, which can be as slippery as ice on a sealed surface.

Logging trucks on West Coast and central North Island roads are wide, fast and cannot move over much. Give them the full lane, slow down when one approaches on a narrow section, and do not attempt to overtake one on a winding road.

Many rural intersections have limited visibility because of hedges and shelter belts. Treat every uncontrolled rural intersection as one where something may emerge, and remember that local drivers know the road and you do not.

sections.heading: Reporting an animal strike
body: Hitting stock is a matter for the farmer and you should stop and report it, both because the animal may need attention and because the owner needs to know. Hitting protected wildlife should be reported to DOC.
Do not attempt to move an injured large animal yourself. Note the location, call it in, and be aware that a live animal on the road is a hazard to the next vehicle as well.
tips: Stop and report stock strikes
Report protected wildlife to DOC
Do not handle injured animals

faq: What animals are a hazard on New Zealand roads?

Livestock above all: sheep and cattle are moved along and across rural roads and a herd on the road is a normal event, not an emergency. Possums and birds are the common night hazard, and swerving for them causes far more harm than hitting them.
What should you do when you meet stock on the road?
Slow right down, stop if the herd is dense, and follow the farmer or the dog's directions rather than trying to pick a way through. Do not sound the horn, which scatters the animals.

camping-rules-local-councils-new-zealand.title: Why camping rules change between New Zealand councils
camping-rules-local-councils-new-zealand.description: District bylaws can define prohibited areas, time limits and sites for vehicles without certification.
camping-rules-local-councils-new-zealand.intro: New Zealand has a national freedom-camping framework but no single nationwide map of every permitted bay. Councils translate local pressure, reserves and infrastructure into bylaws and site notices.

sections.heading: Read the current bylaw
body: Search the official council page for the district, then compare the map, written bylaw and sign at the location. Boundaries can follow reserve parcels rather than obvious roads.
A general app listing should lead to the authority, not replace it. Download the official map before travelling beyond reception.

sections.heading: Understand site-specific differences
body: One council may allow only certified self-contained vehicles, while another names toilets where other campers can stay. Maximum nights, arrival hours and seasonal closures also vary.
Parking rules and freedom-camping rules can both apply. Paying for daytime parking does not automatically buy an overnight right.

sections.heading: When information conflicts
body: Follow the current physical sign and contact the council when online documents disagree. Do not rely on a review written before a bylaw change.
Move to a campground if doubt remains. A legal backup prevents a late search from becoming parking in a prohibited area.

sections.heading: Why the rules differ at every boundary
body: The Freedom Camping Act 2011 lets each territorial authority make its own bylaw for its own district. That is the entire explanation: there are dozens of councils, each responding to different pressure from residents, different site conditions and different enforcement budgets.

The practical consequence is that a rule you confirmed in one district tells you nothing about the next one, and the boundary is frequently invisible from the road. Assuming continuity is the single most common cause of an infringement.
tips: Every council writes its own bylaw
District boundaries are invisible
Never carry a rule across a boundary

sections.heading: The strictest districts
body: Queenstown Lakes, Auckland, Tasman, Thames-Coromandel and Kaikōura all run tight regimes with defined sites, certification requirements, time windows and active patrols. These are also the districts with the highest demand, which is precisely why the rules tightened.

More permissive districts still have prohibited areas and stay limits. Permissive does not mean unregulated, and the sign at the specific location remains the authority regardless of the district's general reputation.

sections.heading: How to check quickly
body: Work out which district you are in, then find that council's freedom camping page or bylaw map. Most publish a map of permitted sites, which is faster to use than reading the bylaw text and is what enforcement officers are working from.

Do this while you still have reception, ideally the evening before rather than at dusk when you are tired and looking for somewhere to stop. Screenshot the map for the district you will be in tomorrow.
tips: Find the council, then the bylaw map
Check the night before, not at dusk
Screenshot the map for tomorrow

sections.heading: When the sign and the map disagree
body: Follow the sign. Councils install temporary restrictions after flooding, slips, events and antisocial behaviour, and those appear physically on the ground long before they reach any published map or third-party dataset.

If a site is full, do not create an overflow line along the access road. That behaviour is what closes sites permanently, and it is the reason a district that was relaxed five years ago is now heavily restricted.

sections.heading: What enforcement actually looks like
body: Officers typically patrol at dusk and again around dawn in high-demand districts, and they check the registration against the self-containment register rather than looking at the sticker. The infringement attaches to the vehicle, so a rental company passes it to you with an administration fee added.
Some councils issue a warning first and others do not, and there is no consistency to rely on. Assume the first contact will be an infringement, because in the busiest districts it usually is.
Disputing one afterwards is difficult without evidence. Photographing the sign when you arrive costs nothing and is the only thing that reliably helps if a dispute arises later.

sections.heading: Why the rules keep tightening
body: Restrictions have expanded over the last decade largely in response to waste, overcrowding and antisocial behaviour at a small number of sites. Councils respond to resident complaints, and closures are usually the end point of a documented problem.
Behaving well is therefore not just courtesy but the mechanism that keeps sites open. The districts with the strictest rules today are the ones where visitor behaviour was worst five years ago.
tips: Rules tighten after complaints
Closures follow documented problems
Behaviour keeps sites open

faq: Why do camping rules change between New Zealand regions?

Because they are set by district and city councils under their own freedom camping bylaws, not by one national rule. Central law, conservation rules and individual site conditions sit on top of that, which is why one layby is legal and the next is not.
How do you find out the camping rules for a specific place?

Read the signage at the site, which is the legally operative version, and check the relevant council's freedom camping bylaw before you rely on a map. An app or a listing tells you what was true when it was compiled.

campervan-budget-new-zealand.title: How to build a New Zealand campervan budget
campervan-budget-new-zealand.description: Rental, fuel, camps, ferry costs and food behave differently, so price each line separately.
campervan-budget-new-zealand.imageAlt: Traveller planning a New Zealand campervan budget
campervan-budget-new-zealand.intro: The advertised daily rate is the smallest interesting number in a campervan budget. Insurance excess, kilometre policy, the ferry, the shape of the route and how often you pay for a powered site will move the total far more than the difference between two rental companies.

sections.heading: Price the vehicle as a complete package
body: Compare quotes on identical dates, vehicle class, insurance excess, kilometre allowance and included equipment. A cheap headline rate with a $5,000 excess and a capped daily kilometre allowance is a different product from a slightly dearer one with a low excess and unlimited kilometres.

Then add the things quoted separately: airport transfers, one-way fees, additional drivers, bedding and kitchen packs, and the cost of reducing the excess. These routinely add several hundred dollars to a fortnight and are invisible in the comparison you started with.
tips: Compare excess, not just daily rate
Check the kilometre allowance
Add one-way and extra-driver fees

sections.heading: Understand the bond and the hold
body: Most operators place a hold on a credit card at pickup, and where the excess is high that hold can be substantial. It is released rather than charged, but it reduces the credit available to you during the trip, which matters if the same card is funding fuel and campsites.

Check whether the operator requires a credit card in the main driver's name, because debit cards are frequently refused. Discovering this at an airport depot at 11pm is a genuinely bad start to a trip.

sections.heading: Turn the route into a fuel number
body: Estimate the actual kilometres of your route rather than using a national average, then add ten to fifteen percent for detours, wrong turns and the drives you have not thought of yet. Multiply distance by the vehicle's litres per 100 kilometres, divide by 100, and multiply by the current price per litre.

A campervan at 12 L/100 km covering 3,000 kilometres uses 360 litres, and that arithmetic dominates the difference between a $15 and a $25 campsite. Fuel is usually the second largest line in the budget and the one people underestimate most.
tips: Add 10 to 15 percent for detours
Use the vehicle's real consumption
Fuel usually beats campsite cost

sections.heading: Correct the estimate early
body: Record the litres and kilometres for your first two fills and recalculate. Loaded weight, headwind, mountain roads, roof boxes and running the engine for heating all push consumption above the brochure figure, sometimes by a quarter.

Remote fuel costs more, and the price varies substantially between a city and a small West Coast or East Cape town. Fill in larger centres where you can, but never pass the last station before a long gap to save a few cents.

sections.heading: Budget the ferry as a fixed block
body: Cook Strait is a large, non-negotiable cost for any trip covering both islands, and it is priced on vehicle length rather than passenger count. A campervan crossing costs several times a car, and a towed trailer or bike rack changes the category again.

Book it early for summer sailings, and read the change and cancellation terms before choosing the cheapest fare. A non-refundable saving disappears the first time weather or a road closure forces a different sailing.
tips: Priced by vehicle size, not people
Book summer sailings early
Cheap fares cost more to change

sections.heading: Mix the overnight styles deliberately
body: A trip built entirely on free sites needs a fully self-sufficient vehicle and still ends up paying for showers, laundry and water somewhere. A trip built entirely on holiday parks costs two or three times as much and gains little on the nights when you arrive late and leave early.

The practical pattern is two or three low-cost DOC or freedom nights followed by one serviced night that resets everything at once: laundry, hot showers, charging, potable water and waste. Costed that way, the serviced night usually earns its rate.

sections.heading: Keep a real contingency
body: Hold money for the things that are not in anyone's plan: a tyre, a windscreen chip, a ferry change, a closed pass that forces a paid night, a day when the weather makes a cabin the sensible choice. A budget with no slack turns every small problem into a decision about whether to continue.

Review your actual spending after three or four days and adjust while the correction is still small. The lines that drift are almost always food, coffee and paid activities rather than accommodation, and they are the easiest to bring back.
tips: Hold a genuine reserve
Review spending in week one
Food and activities drift, not camps

faq: How much does a campervan trip in New Zealand cost per day?

The rental and the fuel dominate, and campsites are usually the smallest line. The guide breaks a realistic day into rental, fuel, camp fees, food and activities, and the gap between the cheapest and the comfortable version is mostly food and activities.
Is a campervan cheaper than car hire plus accommodation?

Over a long trip in summer, usually yes; over a short trip, often not. A campervan carries a higher daily rate and worse fuel consumption, and it pays off only when it is replacing paid accommodation most nights.

cook-strait-ferry-campervan-guide.title: Cook Strait Ferry with a Campervan: Fares and Booking 2026
cook-strait-ferry-campervan-guide.description: Interislander or Bluebridge with a campervan: how vehicle length sets the fare, when to book, check-in and what to do before boarding.
cook-strait-ferry-campervan-guide.imageAlt: Cook Strait ferry entering Picton Harbour
cook-strait-ferry-campervan-guide.intro: The ferry is what turns two island trips into one journey, and it is the least flexible thing in the itinerary. It behaves like a booked transport day rather than a scenic stop, and the two details that cause the most trouble are the vehicle dimensions you declared and what you scheduled immediately afterwards.

sections.heading: Declare the vehicle accurately
body: Fares are set by total length, and total means including everything attached: bike racks, a towbar, an awning that projects, a towed trailer. Under-declaring produces a fare adjustment at check-in and, on a full sailing, occasionally no space at all.

Measure rather than estimate, and if you are collecting a rental, get the dimensions from the operator before booking the crossing. The gap between a car booking and a campervan booking is large enough that guessing is expensive in both directions.
tips: Include racks, boxes and trailers
Get rental dimensions before booking
Under-declaring can cost you the sailing

sections.heading: Choose the operator and sailing sensibly
body: Interislander and Bluebridge both cross Cook Strait, with different terminals in Wellington, slightly different crossing times and different vessels. Neither is universally better; check which terminal suits your route and which sailing times leave you a usable day on the far side.

A crossing consumes most of a day once you include the check-in window, the passage itself and the drive at either end. Treat it as a travel day rather than something you slot between two other drives.

sections.heading: Read the change conditions before you save money
body: The cheapest fares are usually the least flexible, and Cook Strait sailings are cancelled or delayed by weather with some regularity. A saving of forty dollars is poor value if changing the booking costs more than that, which it frequently does.

Where your dates have any uncertainty, particularly in winter or if a long alpine drive precedes the crossing, pay for the flexible fare and record the change deadline against the trip stop rather than trusting your memory of it.
tips: Weather cancellations are routine
Flexible fares are cheap insurance
Note the change deadline on the stop

sections.heading: Do the jobs before the queue
body: Fuel, shop and empty waste tanks before you join the terminal queue. Once you are in line you are committed, the facilities are limited, and the queue can move earlier than expected. Emptying a cassette in Picton because you did not do it in Wellington wastes an hour of your first South Island morning.

Arrive within the operator's stated check-in window, which is earlier than most people assume for vehicles. Have identification and the booking reference ready rather than searching for them at the booth.

sections.heading: Pack what you need for the crossing itself
body: Vehicle deck access is restricted once underway, so anything you want during the passage has to come up with you: medication, warm layers, water, food, a charged phone, and entertainment for children. You cannot go back down for a forgotten jacket.

If anyone in the party is prone to seasickness, take something before boarding rather than after the ship starts moving. Cook Strait can be genuinely rough, and the strait is at its worst in a southerly.
tips: No deck access once underway
Take medication before boarding
Warm layers, water and chargers up top

sections.heading: Protect the day after arrival
body: The single most common ferry mistake is booking something expensive and unmissable immediately after the scheduled arrival. A delayed sailing then costs you a tour, a booking or a long drive done in the dark. Leave the following block soft.

Avoid scheduling a long alpine drive or a difficult road straight off the ship, particularly on an evening sailing. Queen Charlotte Drive is beautiful and slow, and it is not a road to meet for the first time while tired at dusk.

sections.heading: Use Picton or Wellington as a recovery night
body: Book a night close to the terminal on the arrival side when the sailing lands late. A short drive to a known campground beats pushing on towards a site hours away, and it means the next morning starts properly rather than as damage control.
The same applies before an early sailing. A night near the terminal is worth more than a slightly better site an hour away, because a missed check-in window is a missed crossing.
tips: Stay near the terminal for late arrivals
Do not drive far after an evening sailing
Miss the window, miss the sailing

faq: Do you need to book the Cook Strait ferry in advance for a campervan?
Yes, and earlier than you would expect. Vehicle space is limited, campervans take a larger and separately priced slot, and summer sailings sell out weeks ahead.
How long does the Cook Strait crossing take?

About three and a half hours between Wellington and Picton, plus check-in an hour or more beforehand for a vehicle. Sailings are cancelled in heavy weather often enough that a same-day connection on either side is a bad plan.

new-zealand-driving-day-planner.title: How long should a New Zealand driving day be?
new-zealand-driving-day-planner.description: Mountain roads, one-lane bridges and scenic stops make kilometres a poor measure of effort.
new-zealand-driving-day-planner.imageAlt: Winding New Zealand road through hills
new-zealand-driving-day-planner.intro: New Zealand roads punish itineraries built from distance. Two hundred and fifty kilometres is an easy morning on a straight road and a full, tiring day through coastal bends and one-lane bridges. Plan from the character of the road and the daylight available, and use kilometres only as a first sanity check.

sections.heading: Moving time is not day length
body: Take the routing estimate as a floor, then add everything else the day contains: fuel, groceries, coffee, roadworks, viewpoints, a short walk, photographs and the time spent finding and setting up tonight's site. Packing camp in the morning is another half hour nobody budgets for.

A realistic multiplier is around one and a half times the navigation estimate for a touring day with stops. If that produces something uncomfortable, the answer is a shorter leg rather than a faster one.
tips: Add 50 percent to routing estimates
Packing camp costs real time
Finding a site takes longer than you think

sections.heading: Three to four hours is a comfortable day
body: Most people who travel New Zealand for more than a week settle on three to four hours of driving as the point where the trip stays enjoyable. Beyond that, the stops get skipped, the walks get dropped, and the day becomes about arriving rather than travelling.

Occasional longer days are fine, especially on the straighter stretches of Canterbury or the central North Island. Consecutive long days are what produce fatigue, and fatigue is the underlying cause of a large share of visitor crashes here.

sections.heading: Some roads take far longer than they look
body: The Coromandel coast, Tākaka Hill, Queen Charlotte Drive, the Catlins, the Milford Road and much of the West Coast are all slower than their distances suggest, even fully sealed. Tight corners, camber, single-lane bridges and scenery that makes everyone want to stop combine to stretch a two-hour estimate well past three.

Add an unfamiliar campervan and it stretches again. Width, height, braking distance and cornering all need practice, and the first two days in a large vehicle are noticeably slower than the rest of the trip.
tips: Coastal roads run well over estimate
Campervans are slower for two days
One-lane bridges break your rhythm

sections.heading: One-lane bridges and gravel
body: One-lane bridges are common, particularly on the West Coast and in Northland, and the priority is signed rather than assumed: the larger arrow is your direction of priority. Some are shared with rail. Slow, look through, and be prepared to wait rather than racing to claim the bridge.

Do not take an unsealed shortcut just because it is shorter. Rental agreements frequently prohibit specific gravel roads, insurance may not cover damage on them, and a road that is fine in a dry February is a different proposition after rain.

sections.heading: Plan around daylight, not the clock
body: In midwinter the usable light in the south is roughly nine hours, and even in summer a valley loses the sun long before the official sunset. Work backwards from the time you want to be parked, not forwards from when you hope to leave.
Set a turnaround time for any walk and honour it. Most of the trouble people get into on New Zealand tracks comes from continuing past the point where the return trip fits in the light remaining.
tips: Work backwards from arrival time
Valleys lose light early
Set a turnaround time for walks

sections.heading: Dawn and dusk are the difficult hours
body: Low sun on a wet road removes visibility almost completely, and it arrives at exactly the times you are most likely to be driving if the day has slipped. Possums, hares and stock are also most active around dawn and dusk, and swerving for an animal causes more serious crashes than hitting one.
Aim to be off the road, or at least on an easy stretch of it, during those hours. Arriving in daylight also means you can inspect the pitch, check access and level the vehicle without a head torch.

sections.heading: Recover a slipping day by cutting, not accelerating
